topics.ANAT: Anatomy: Waldeyer's ring, oropharynx, innervation & pharyngeal spaces
topics.OSA: OSA: risk factors, features, screening & diagnosis

cards.q: What is Waldeyer's ring, and what are its components and their positions?
cards.a:
• **Incomplete ring of MALT** (T cells, B cells, macrophages) guarding the entrance to the aerodigestive tract
• **Pharyngeal tonsil (adenoid)** – roof and posterior wall of nasopharynx (superior)
• **Tubal tonsils** – around the Eustachian tube openings, near the salpingopharyngeal fold (lateral, upper)
• **Palatine tonsils** – tonsillar fossae of the oropharynx (lateral)
• **Lingual tonsil** – base (posterior 1/3) of tongue (inferior)
• First-line defence against inhaled and ingested pathogens
cards.m: Clock face from above: adenoid at 12, tubal tonsils at 2 and 10, palatine tonsils at 3 and 9, lingual tonsil at 6.

cards.q: Where exactly does the palatine tonsil sit, and what forms its bed?
cards.a:
• Lies in the **tonsillar fossa** on each side of the oropharynx
• **Anterior pillar = palatoglossal arch**; **posterior pillar = palatopharyngeal arch**
• Lateral bed: tonsillar capsule on the **superior constrictor** muscle
• Potential **peritonsillar space** between capsule and superior constrictor = site of quinsy
• Most commonly infected and surgically removed part of Waldeyer's ring
cards.m: Pillars in alphabetical order front to back: palatoGlossal before palatoPharyngeal (G before P).

cards.q: What are the boundaries of the oropharynx?
cards.a:
• **Superior:** soft palate / pharyngeal isthmus (opens into nasopharynx)
• **Inferior:** upper border of the epiglottis (opens into laryngopharynx)
• **Anterior:** oropharyngeal isthmus and **posterior 1/3 of tongue**
• **Posterior:** posterior pharyngeal wall in front of **C2-C3**
• **Lateral:** palatine tonsils and palatopharyngeal arches
• Key structures: base of tongue, lingual tonsils, palatine tonsils, superior constrictor
cards.m: Oropharynx spans soft palate to tip of epiglottis – the part you see when the patient says 'Ahh'.

cards.q: What is the arterial supply and venous drainage of the palatine tonsil, and which vessels bleed after tonsillectomy?
cards.a:
• Arteries: **tonsillar branch of facial artery (main supply)**, ascending palatine, ascending pharyngeal, dorsal lingual, lesser palatine
• Veins: **paratonsillar (external palatine) vein** → pterygoid plexus above and facial / internal jugular vein below
• Post-tonsillectomy bleeding usually comes from the **paratonsillar vein** or the **tonsillar artery** at the lower pole
• The **internal carotid artery** lies about 2.5 cm posterolateral to the tonsil – relevant in deep neck abscesses
cards.m: Five arteries, one main: the Facial artery Feeds the tonsil.

cards.q: Where does the palatine tonsil drain lymph, and which node enlarges in tonsillitis?
cards.a:
• Main drainage: **jugulodigastric (upper deep cervical) node** – the 'tonsillar node' below the angle of the mandible
• Also retropharyngeal nodes (posterior pharyngeal wall, adenoids)
• Enlarged, tender jugulodigastric node is a classic sign of acute tonsillitis; suppuration → cervical abscess
• Note: slide p11 lists only retropharyngeal nodes; the tonsil drains mainly to the jugulodigastric node (as p22 states)
cards.m: Feel just below the angle of the jaw – the jugulodigastric node is the tonsil's sentry.

cards.q: Which nerve gives sensation to the oropharynx and tonsil, and why does tonsil disease cause earache?
cards.a:
• **Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)** is the main sensory nerve: oropharyngeal mucosa, palatine tonsil, posterior 1/3 of tongue, soft palate
• CN IX also supplies the middle ear via its **tympanic branch (Jacobson's nerve)**
• So tonsillitis, quinsy, tonsillar carcinoma and post-tonsillectomy pain are felt as **referred otalgia**
• Earache with a normal ear drum in an adult smoker → examine the oropharynx for cancer
cards.m: IX = Ear and Throat on one wire: pain in the tonsil rings in the ear.

cards.q: What is the motor nerve supply of the soft palate and pharynx?
cards.a:
• **Pharyngeal plexus** – fibres of the **vagus (CN X)** with the cranial accessory (CN XI)
• Supplies pharyngeal constrictors, palatopharyngeus, salpingopharyngeus, levator veli palatini, uvular muscle, palatoglossus
• **Exception: tensor veli palatini** – supplied by the **mandibular nerve (CN V3)** via the nerve to medial pterygoid
• Stylopharyngeus is the only pharyngeal muscle supplied by **CN IX**
cards.m: 'Tensor is the Trigeminal one' – both start with T.

cards.q: How is sensation and taste supplied to the tongue?
cards.a:
• **Anterior 2/3:** general sensation **lingual nerve (V3)**; taste **chorda tympani (VII)**
• **Posterior 1/3:** general sensation **and** taste **glossopharyngeal (IX)**
• **Epiglottic region / vallecula:** sensation and taste **internal laryngeal nerve (X)**
• Clinical: base-of-tongue cancer → referred otalgia via IX
cards.m: Front of tongue borrows two nerves (V for touch, VII for taste); the back does both with one (IX).

cards.q: What supplies the muscles of the tongue, and what is the exception?
cards.a:
• All intrinsic and extrinsic tongue muscles: **hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)**
• **Exception: palatoglossus** – supplied by the **vagus (CN X)** via the pharyngeal plexus (it is really a palatal muscle)
• XII palsy (LMN): tongue deviates **towards** the side of the lesion, with wasting and fasciculation
cards.m: Palatoglossus belongs to the Palate gang, so it takes the palate's nerve – X, not XII.

cards.q: What is the gag reflex, what triggers it and what are its nerve pathways?
cards.a:
• Involuntary bilateral contraction of pharyngeal muscles and elevation of the soft palate to prevent choking on foreign material
• Trigger: touching the **posterior pharyngeal wall, tonsillar pillars or base of tongue**
• **Afferent: CN IX**; **efferent: CN X**
• Absent gag on one side → think IX / X lesion (e.g. post-styloid parapharyngeal pathology, jugular foramen)
cards.m: Gag goes in on IX, out on X – 'nine in, ten out'.

cards.q: Describe the parapharyngeal space: shape, extent, boundaries and connections.
cards.a:
• **Inverted pyramid**: base at the **skull base**, apex at the **hyoid** bone
• **Medial:** buccopharyngeal fascia over the superior constrictor (pharynx/tonsil)
• **Lateral:** superficial layer of deep cervical fascia over the medial pterygoid, mandible and parotid
• Connects **posteriorly with the retropharyngeal space** and **anteriorly with the submandibular space**
• Infection reaches it from **teeth, tonsils/pharynx, maxilla or mandible**
cards.m: Upside-down pyramid hanging from the skull base beside the throat, pointing down at the hyoid.

cards.q: What are the boundaries of the retropharyngeal space, and why is the danger space so called?
cards.a:
• Retropharyngeal space: **anterior** – buccopharyngeal fascia (behind pharynx); **posterior** – **alar fascia**
• Extends from **skull base** down into the upper mediastinum; contains retropharyngeal nodes
• **Danger space** lies between the **alar** and **prevertebral** fascia and runs from skull base to the **diaphragm**
• Infection: Waldeyer's ring / dental focus → retropharyngeal space → danger space → **mediastinitis**
• Note: slide p38 calls the posterior boundary prevertebral fascia; correct is alar fascia (as p12 states)
cards.m: Front to back: pharynx – retropharyngeal space – Alar – DANGER – Prevertebral – spine. Danger is sandwiched between A and P.

cards.q: What are the functions of the oropharynx?
cards.a:
• **Common conduit** for air (to lungs) and food (to oesophagus)
• **Deglutition** – the pharyngeal phase of swallowing
• **Local defence and immunity** – Waldeyer's ring
• **Part of the vocal tract** – resonance and articulation
• **Taste** – posterior 1/3 of tongue and epiglottic region
cards.m: 'CRISP-T': Conduit, Resonance, Immunity, Swallowing, Protection of airway, Taste.

cards.q: What happens in the oral phase of swallowing?
cards.a:
• **Voluntary** phase
• **Preparatory:** food + saliva form a bolus; bolus held on the tongue against the hard palate; soft palate and tongue rest down (seals the back of the mouth)
• **Propulsion:** tongue presses on the palate from front to back, pushing the bolus backwards
• Oropharyngeal isthmus then opens to receive the bolus
• **Breathing continues** during the oral phase
cards.m: Oral phase = you are still in charge; once the bolus touches the pillars, the reflex takes over.

cards.q: What are the key events of the pharyngeal phase of swallowing?
cards.a:
• **Involuntary** reflex; two jobs: **move the bolus** and **protect the airway**
• **Soft palate rises** to close the nasopharynx (prevents nasal regurgitation)
• **Larynx elevates**, **epiglottis folds back** over the inlet, **vocal cords close** = **deglutition apnoea**
• **Upper oesophageal sphincter (cricopharyngeus) relaxes**
• Tongue pushes the bolus down and **pharyngeal constrictors contract sequentially**
cards.m: Shut the three doors – nose (soft palate), larynx (epiglottis + cords) – and open the fourth (UES).

cards.q: Which phases of swallowing are voluntary, and what happens in the oesophageal phase?
cards.a:
• **Oral – voluntary**; **pharyngeal – involuntary (reflex)**; **oesophageal – involuntary**
• Oesophageal phase: **peristalsis** carries the bolus down; lower oesophageal sphincter relaxes
• After the bolus passes, the epiglottis returns upright and the airway reopens
• Clinical: pharyngeal-phase failure (e.g. IX/X palsy) causes **aspiration** and nasal regurgitation
cards.m: One voluntary, two automatic – you choose to swallow, then the body finishes the job.

cards.q: How do the tonsils generate mucosal immunity?
cards.a:
• **M cells** over the tonsillar crypts capture antigens and deliver them to the underlying lymphoid tissue
• Activates **T and B lymphocytes**
• **B cells → secretory IgA** (mucosal protection); IgM and IgG neutralise bacteria, viruses and fungi
• **T cells** → cell-mediated immunity
• Tonsils are most active in childhood – why they enlarge physiologically up to about 7-8 years
cards.m: M cells are the Mailmen: they post antigens from the crypt surface to the lymphocytes below.

cards.q: How is tonsillitis classified by duration, and what defines recurrent tonsillitis (Paradise criteria)?
cards.a:
• **Acute:** < 2 weeks
• **Chronic:** persistent > 3 months
• **Recurrent (Paradise criteria):** **≥ 7 episodes in 1 year**, or **≥ 5/year for 2 years**, or **≥ 3/year for 3 years**
• Recurrent episodes meeting these criteria are the commonest indication for tonsillectomy
cards.m: 7-5-3: seven in one, five for two, three for three.

cards.q: What organisms cause acute tonsillitis?
cards.a:
• **Viral (~70%, commonest, usually milder):** adenovirus, rhinovirus, influenza, EBV, HSV, CMV
• **Main bacterial cause: group A β-haemolytic Streptococcus (S. pyogenes)**
• Others: Staphylococcus aureus, pneumococcus, H. influenzae
• Note: slide p21 lists staphylococcus first; the main bacterial cause is group A Streptococcus (as p22 states)
cards.m: Most sore throats are viral; the bacterium to treat and fear is GAS – Group A Strep (rheumatic fever).

cards.q: What are the symptoms of acute tonsillitis, and who does it affect?
cards.a:
• Mainly **school-aged children** and adults under 50; rare in infants
• **Sore throat**, **odynophagia / dysphagia**, **fever** (may be high in children)
• **Earache** – referred via CN IX, or due to coexisting AOM
• Constitutional: headache, body ache, malaise
• Young children may present with vomiting, abdominal pain or refusing feeds
cards.m: Throat, fever, ear – the classic triad of a child with tonsillitis.

cards.q: What examination findings support acute tonsillitis?
cards.a:
• **Foetid breath** and coated tongue
• Hyperaemia of the pillars, soft palate and uvula
• Tonsils **red and swollen**; yellow spots of pus at crypt openings (follicular) or a whitish membrane (membranous)
• **Enlarged, tender jugulodigastric nodes**
• Check for asymmetry, uvula deviation and trismus – these point to quinsy rather than simple tonsillitis
cards.m: Look in the mouth, then feel the neck – the tender jugulodigastric node confirms it.

cards.q: What are the four clinical types of acute tonsillitis?
cards.a:
• **Catarrhal (superficial):** surface epithelium only, part of generalised pharyngitis, usually **viral**
• **Follicular:** infection in the crypts → **yellowish spots of pus** at crypt openings
• **Parenchymatous:** whole tonsil uniformly enlarged, red, congested – may **meet in the midline**
• **Membranous:** exudate from crypts coalesces into a whitish membrane that is **easily wiped away**
cards.m: CFPM – going deeper and wider: Catarrhal (surface) → Follicular (crypts) → Parenchymatous (whole tonsil) → Membranous (coalesced).

cards.q: Which clinical scores help decide on antibiotics in sore throat?
cards.a:
• **Centor:** fever > 38 °C, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical nodes, **absence of cough** (1 point each)
• **McIsaac** adds age: +1 if 3-14 y, −1 if ≥ 45 y
• **FeverPAIN:** Fever, Purulence, Attend rapidly (≤ 3 days), Inflamed tonsils, No cough/coryza
• Centor 3-4 or FeverPAIN ≥ 4 → bacterial infection more likely → consider antibiotics
• Low scores → analgesia, fluids, no antibiotic (most are viral)
cards.m: Centor = 'no cough plus three signs'; cough and coryza point to a virus.

cards.q: How do you treat acute bacterial tonsillitis?
cards.a:
• Bed rest, **plenty of oral fluids**, warm saline gargles
• Analgesia: **paracetamol ± NSAID** (e.g. ibuprofen)
• **Penicillin V for 10 days** – drug of choice; full course eradicates group A Strep (prevents rheumatic fever)
• Penicillin allergy: **erythromycin / other macrolide**
• **Avoid amoxicillin/ampicillin** if infectious mononucleosis is possible (rash)
• Note: slide p28 says 'aspirin or paracetamol'; **avoid aspirin** in children (Reye syndrome) and in anyone who may need tonsil surgery (bleeding)
cards.m: Pen V for ten: 'P-10'. Aspirin = Reye's + bleeding – keep it off the throat ward.

cards.q: What are the differential diagnoses of a membrane over the tonsil?
cards.a:
• **Membranous tonsillitis**
• **Diphtheria**
• **Vincent's angina**
• **Infectious mononucleosis**
• **Agranulocytosis**, **leukaemia**
• **Aphthous ulcers**, **traumatic ulcer**, **candidal infection**
• **Malignancy of the tonsil**
cards.m: Sort the list into three bins: Infection (tonsillitis, diphtheria, Vincent, IM, Candida), Blood (agranulocytosis, leukaemia), Ulcer/tumour (aphthous, traumatic, malignancy).

cards.q: How does diphtheria differ from membranous tonsillitis, and how is it managed?
cards.a:
• **Corynebacterium diphtheriae**; unvaccinated child; insidious, low-grade fever but very toxic
• **Greyish-white membrane extending beyond the tonsil** onto pillars, soft palate and uvula
• **Adherent – bleeds when removed** (tonsillitis membrane wipes off easily)
• **Bull neck** (marked nodes and oedema); risks: airway obstruction, myocarditis, palatal/nerve palsy
• Management: isolate, **notify (notifiable in Malaysia)**, throat swab, **antitoxin** urgently + **penicillin or erythromycin**, airway care, trace and treat contacts
cards.m: Diphtheria: Dirty grey, Doesn't wipe off, Drips blood, Deadly toxin.

cards.q: What features point to infectious mononucleosis in a patient with membranous tonsillitis?
cards.a:
• **EBV**; adolescent / young adult
• Prolonged fever, malaise, very enlarged tonsils with membrane
• **Generalised lymphadenopathy** (posterior cervical), **splenomegaly**, **palatal petechiae**
• FBC: **lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes**; **Monospot / Paul-Bunnell** (heterophile antibodies), EBV serology
• **Amoxicillin/ampicillin → widespread maculopapular rash**
• Advise **no contact sports for ~4-6 weeks** (splenic rupture); steroids if airway threatened
cards.m: 'Kissing disease': big tonsils, big nodes, big spleen – and an amoxicillin rash.

cards.q: What is Vincent's angina?
cards.a:
• Ulceromembranous tonsillitis / gingivitis due to **fusiform bacilli + spirochaetes** (Borrelia vincentii)
• Associated with **poor oral hygiene**, malnutrition, debilitated patients
• **Painful ulcer covered by a membrane** that leaves a bleeding ulcer when removed; often unilateral; foul breath, bleeding gums
• Diagnosis: smear of the membrane
• Treatment: **penicillin and/or metronidazole**, oral hygiene, hydrogen peroxide mouthwash
cards.m: Vincent = Very poor oral hygiene + Vermicular spirochaetes.

cards.q: Which membrane or ulcer on the tonsil demands a full blood count or a biopsy?
cards.a:
• **Agranulocytosis** (drug-induced, e.g. carbimazole) and **acute leukaemia** – necrotic ulcer/membrane, minimal pus, sepsis, bruising → **urgent FBC**
• **Malignancy** – **unilateral**, ulcerated, indurated or enlarging tonsil, often an **older smoker/drinker**, referred otalgia, neck node → **biopsy**
• Any 'tonsillitis' not responding to antibiotics, or unilateral, is not simple tonsillitis
cards.m: Bilateral and young = infection; unilateral and old = cancer until proven otherwise.

cards.q: What causes chronic tonsillitis, and what are its types?
cards.a:
• Complication of **repeated acute tonsillitis**, or **subclinical** infection of the tonsil
• Predisposed by chronic infection in the **sinuses and teeth**
• Mainly **children and young adults**; rare > 50 years
• Types: **chronic follicular** (crypts full of infected cheesy material), **chronic parenchymatous** (hyperplasia, large tonsils), **chronic fibroid** (small but infected tonsils)
cards.m: Chronic types = 'Follicles, Flesh, Fibrosis'.

cards.q: What are the clinical features and treatment of chronic tonsillitis?
cards.a:
• Symptoms: **recurrent sore throat**, chronic throat irritation with cough, **bad taste / halitosis** (pus in crypts), thick speech, dysphagia, choking spells at night
• Signs: varying enlargement; **yellow beads of pus**; small tonsils where pressure on the anterior pillar **expresses cheesy material**; **flushed anterior pillars**; enlarged jugulodigastric nodes
• Treatment: conservative – general health, diet, treat teeth, nose and sinus infection
• **Tonsillectomy** if recurrent attacks or tonsils interfere with speech, swallowing or breathing
cards.m: Chronic tonsillitis smells before it hurts – halitosis and cheesy crypts.

cards.q: What are the complications of acute tonsillitis?
cards.a:
• **Local / suppurative:** chronic tonsillitis, **peritonsillar abscess**, **parapharyngeal abscess**, **cervical abscess** (suppuration of jugulodigastric node), **acute otitis media**
• **Systemic / non-suppurative (GAS):** **rheumatic fever**, **acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis**, scarlet fever
• **Subacute bacterial endocarditis** (Streptococcus viridans) in valvular heart disease
cards.m: Spreads around (abscesses, ear) or stirs the immune system (heart, joints, kidneys).

cards.q: What are tonsillolith, tonsillar cyst and intratonsillar abscess?
cards.a:
• **Tonsillolith:** blocked crypt → debris accumulates → **calcium and magnesium salts** deposit → stone that enlarges and may ulcerate through; causes halitosis, foreign body feeling
• **Tonsillar cyst:** blocked crypt → yellowish swelling over the tonsil; usually **symptomless**; easily drained
• **Intratonsillar abscess:** pus **within** the tonsil – swollen, red, local pain and dysphagia; drain ± tonsillectomy
cards.m: All three start with a blocked crypt: stone (salts), sac (cyst) or pus (abscess).

cards.q: What are the absolute indications for tonsillectomy?
cards.a:
• **Recurrent throat infection** meeting **Paradise criteria** (7 in 1 y / 5 per y for 2 y / 3 per y for 3 y)
• **Peritonsillar abscess** – children after the first episode; adults after a second episode
• Tonsillitis causing **febrile seizures**
• **Obstructive hypertrophy** → sleep-disordered breathing / **OSA**, dysphagia, **cor pulmonale**
• **Suspected malignancy** – e.g. **unilateral tonsillar enlargement** (excision biopsy)
cards.m: 'Recurrent, Abscess, Seizures, Obstruction, Malignancy' – RASOM.

cards.q: What are the relative indications for tonsillectomy, and other uses of the operation?
cards.a:
• Relative: **diphtheria carriers** and **streptococcal carriers** not cleared by antibiotics
• **Chronic tonsillitis** with halitosis and cheesy crypts unresponsive to treatment
• **Recurrent streptococcal tonsillitis in valvular heart disease** (risk of rheumatic fever / endocarditis)
• As part of another operation: **uvulopalatopharyngoplasty**, **glossopharyngeal neurectomy**, **removal of an elongated styloid process** (Eagle syndrome)
cards.m: Relative = carriers, chronic smell, cardiac risk; 'access' = the tonsil is in the way of another operation.

cards.q: What are the contraindications to tonsillectomy?
cards.a:
• **Acute infection** of the tonsils – wait **2-3 weeks** (more bleeding when inflamed)
• **Bleeding disorder** (haemophilia, von Willebrand disease, leukaemia) until corrected
• **Cleft palate / submucous cleft** – risk of velopharyngeal insufficiency (nasal speech)
• **Anaemia** (Hb < 10 g/dL) and uncontrolled systemic disease (diabetes, hypertension, heart disease)
• Old teaching: avoid during **polio epidemics** (bulbar polio)
cards.m: Before you cut, check: infection, blood (clotting + Hb), cleft, systemic disease.

cards.q: In what position is tonsillectomy performed, and why?
cards.a:
• **Rose's position:** supine, **head extended** with a sandbag/pad under the shoulders
• Mouth held open with a **Boyle-Davis mouth gag**
• Extension lets **blood pool in the nasopharynx** rather than run into the larynx (airway protected; cuffed tube in place)
• Gives the surgeon a direct view of the tonsillar fossae
• Techniques: cold steel dissection, bipolar diathermy, coblation
cards.m: Rose's position: chin to the ceiling, blood to the nasopharynx, not the larynx.

cards.q: What is primary (reactionary) post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage, and how is it managed?
cards.a:
• Bleeding within **24 hours**, usually in the **first few hours** after surgery
• Cause: slipped ligature, rise in BP on waking, unsecured vessel (**paratonsillar vein**, tonsillar branch of facial artery)
• Signs: frequent swallowing, vomiting dark blood, tachycardia, pallor – children hide blood loss
• Management: resuscitate (IV access, group and crossmatch), sit up, remove clot, pressure/adrenaline swab
• Persistent bleeding → **return to theatre** for haemostasis under GA (beware stomach full of blood)
cards.m: Reactionary = Reaction to the operation (first 24 h) → Return to theatre.

cards.q: What is secondary post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage, and how is it managed?
cards.a:
• Bleeding at **day 5-10** post-operatively
• Cause: **infection of the tonsillar bed** with slough separation
• Management: **admit**, IV access, FBC and group and save, **IV antibiotics**, hydrogen peroxide gargles
• Most settle; heavy or persistent bleeding → **return to theatre**
• Advise all patients at discharge to return immediately if any bleeding occurs
cards.m: Secondary = Septic, Seven-ish days (5-10).

cards.q: Apart from haemorrhage, what are the complications of tonsillectomy?
cards.a:
• **Pain** and **referred otalgia** (CN IX) – peaks around day 3-5; regular analgesia
• **Dehydration** from poor oral intake – encourage eating and drinking normally
• Airway: laryngospasm, aspiration of blood, obstruction (especially in OSA children – monitor overnight)
• Injury: teeth, lips, uvula, soft palate, temporomandibular joint (gag)
• Infection of tonsillar bed, velopharyngeal insufficiency, rarely **ICA injury**
• Anaesthetic complications
cards.m: After tonsils: Pain, Ear pain, Poor drinking, Puffy airway.

cards.q: What is a peritonsillar abscess (quinsy), and where exactly is the pus?
cards.a:
• Collection of pus in the **peritonsillar space**
• Between the **tonsillar capsule** and the **superior constrictor** muscle
• Usually at the **upper pole**, in the soft palate above the tonsil
• Almost always **unilateral**
• Commonest deep neck space infection in **adults**
cards.m: Quinsy pus sits outside the capsule but inside the constrictor – 'between the coat and the wall'.

cards.q: How does a quinsy develop, and who gets it?
cards.a:
• Sequence: infected tonsillar crypt (often near the **Weber glands** at the upper pole) → **intratonsillar abscess** → bursts through the capsule → **peritonsillitis (cellulitis)** → **peritonsillar abscess**
• Usually follows acute tonsillitis; may arise **de novo** without preceding sore throat
• **Common in adults**, rare in children even though tonsillitis is common in children
• Risk factors: **smoking**, **previous quinsy**
cards.m: Crypt → inside tonsil → through capsule → cellulitis → abscess: five steps from sore throat to quinsy.

cards.q: Which organisms cause peritonsillar abscess?
cards.a:
• **Mixed aerobic and anaerobic** infection
• Aerobes: **Streptococcus pyogenes** (commonest), Staphylococcus aureus, H. influenzae
• Anaerobes: **Bacteroides** species, Fusobacterium
• Hence antibiotic must cover anaerobes: **co-amoxiclav**, or penicillin + **metronidazole**
cards.m: Quinsy is a mixed bag – always cover anaerobes.

cards.q: What are the symptoms of a quinsy, and why do trismus and earache occur?
cards.a:
• General: fever, chills and rigors, malaise, headache, body ache, nausea
• Local: **severe unilateral throat pain**, **odynophagia** (cannot swallow saliva – **drooling**), **dehydration**
• **'Hot potato' voice** – muffled, thick speech
• **Trismus** – spasm of the **medial pterygoid** irritated by pus lateral to the constrictor
• **Unilateral earache** – referred via **CN IX**
• Foul breath
cards.m: Quinsy 'T's: Tonsil pain one side, Trismus, Thick (hot potato) voice, Tympanic referred pain.

cards.q: What are the examination findings in a quinsy?
cards.a:
• **Bulging of the soft palate and anterior pillar above the tonsil** on the affected side
• **Uvula oedematous and deviated to the OPPOSITE side**
• Tonsil congested, swollen and pushed **downwards and medially**; mucopus over the tonsillar region
• Trismus limits the view
• **Cervical lymphadenopathy**; **torticollis** towards the affected side
cards.m: The pus pushes the uvula away – it points to the healthy side.

cards.q: How do you tell peritonsillitis (cellulitis) from a peritonsillar abscess?
cards.a:
• Clinically similar: unilateral pain, palatal swelling, trismus
• Abscess favoured by: marked **bulge with fluctuance**, uvula deviation, worsening despite 24-48 h IV antibiotics
• **Needle aspiration** at the point of maximum bulge: pus = abscess; no pus = peritonsillitis (or abscess missed)
• **CECT neck** if diagnosis unclear, aspiration dry, or deeper (parapharyngeal) spread suspected
• Peritonsillitis: IV antibiotics, fluids, analgesia; abscess: drain + antibiotics
cards.m: Needle settles the argument: pus or no pus.

cards.q: What investigations are done in a quinsy?
cards.a:
• **Pus for culture and sensitivity** (from aspiration or I&D)
• **CECT neck** if parapharyngeal/deep neck extension, failure to improve, or unclear diagnosis
• FBC (leucocytosis), renal profile (dehydration), glucose (diabetes)
• Consider Monospot / EBV serology in young adults with atypical features
cards.m: Get the pus, and scan if it may have gone deep.

cards.q: What is the medical management of a quinsy?
cards.a:
• **Admit**; **IV fluid replacement** (patient often cannot swallow)
• **IV co-amoxiclav (Augmentin) 1.2 g TDS** – or IV benzylpenicillin + metronidazole; clindamycin if penicillin-allergic
• **Analgesia** (paracetamol, NSAID) and a **corticosteroid** (e.g. single dose of IV dexamethasone) to reduce pain, swelling and trismus
• **Oral hygiene:** hydrogen peroxide or saline mouthwash
• Switch to oral antibiotics to complete the course once eating
cards.m: Fluids, Augmentin, painkiller, steroid – then let the knife do the rest.

cards.q: How is a quinsy drained, and when is tonsillectomy done?
cards.a:
• Under **local anaesthetic**, patient sitting up with suction ready
• **Needle aspiration** or **incision and drainage** at the **point of maximum bulge** – above the upper pole, where a horizontal line through the **base of the uvula** meets a vertical line along the **anterior pillar**
• Keep the blade guarded (shallow incision) – the ICA lies posterolateral
• Followed by warm salt-water gargles
• **Interval tonsillectomy** about **4-6 weeks** later; or **hot (abscess) tonsillectomy** in selected cases
cards.m: Cross-hairs: base of uvula across, anterior pillar down – aim where they meet.

cards.q: What are the complications of a peritonsillar abscess?
cards.a:
• Early: **parapharyngeal abscess**, **laryngeal oedema** (airway obstruction), **septicaemia**
• Aspiration of pus → **pneumonitis / lung abscess** (spontaneous rupture during sleep)
• **Internal jugular vein thrombophlebitis** (Lemierre syndrome – Fusobacterium, septic emboli)
• **Spontaneous haemorrhage** from erosion of the carotid artery or jugular vein
• Late: **recurrent quinsy** and recurrent tonsillitis
cards.m: Quinsy can spread Out (parapharyngeal), Down (larynx, lungs) or into Vessels (IJV, carotid).

cards.q: How is the parapharyngeal space divided, and what does the prestyloid compartment contain?
cards.a:
• The **styloid process and its muscles** divide it into **prestyloid (anterior)** and **poststyloid (posterior)** compartments
• **Prestyloid** contents: mostly **fat**; **deep lobe of parotid**; **internal maxillary artery**; branches of **V3** (inferior alveolar, lingual, auriculotemporal nerves); styloglossus and stylopharyngeus
• Prestyloid infection lies next to the **medial pterygoid** → trismus
cards.m: Prestyloid = 'Fat, Parotid, Maxillary artery, V3' – soft stuff in front.

cards.q: What does the poststyloid compartment contain, and why does it matter?
cards.a:
• **Internal carotid artery**, **internal jugular vein**
• **Cranial nerves IX, X, XI, XII**
• **Cervical sympathetic chain**; associated lymph nodes
• Clinical: infection here can cause **IX-XII palsies**, **Horner syndrome**, **IJV thrombophlebitis** and **carotid erosion / haemorrhage**
cards.m: Poststyloid = the carotid sheath crowd: 'Carotid, Jugular, 9-10-11-12, Sympathetic'.

cards.q: What are the sources of a parapharyngeal abscess?
cards.a:
• **Pharynx:** acute/chronic tonsillitis and adenoiditis, **bursting of a peritonsillar abscess**
• **Teeth:** dental infection, especially lower third molar
• **Ear:** **Bezold abscess**, petrositis
• **Other spaces:** parotid, retropharyngeal and submandibular infections
• **Trauma:** penetrating neck injury, LA injection for tonsillectomy or **inferior alveolar (mandibular) nerve block**
cards.m: 'PTEST': Pharynx, Teeth, Ear, Spaces, Trauma.

cards.q: What are the clinical features of a parapharyngeal abscess, anterior versus posterior compartment?
cards.a:
• General: fever, sore throat, odynophagia, **torticollis**, pain and swelling
• **Anterior (prestyloid):** **prolapse of the tonsil and tonsillar fossa** medially, **trismus**, external swelling **behind the angle of the jaw**
• **Posterior (poststyloid):** **bulge of the pharynx behind the posterior pillar**, swelling of the parotid region, **paralysis of CN IX, X, XI, XII**, Horner syndrome
• Little or no trismus in poststyloid abscess
cards.m: Anterior = Angle-of-jaw swelling + trismus; Posterior = Palsies (IX-XII).

cards.q: How do you distinguish a parapharyngeal abscess from a quinsy on examination?
cards.a:
• Quinsy: swelling **above** the tonsil in the soft palate; uvula markedly deviated; little external neck swelling
• Parapharyngeal abscess: tonsil itself often **looks normal** but the **tonsil and lateral pharyngeal wall are pushed medially**
• Parapharyngeal: firm **swelling behind the angle of the mandible**, torticollis, may have **cranial nerve palsies**
• Both have trismus; CECT confirms which space is involved
cards.m: Quinsy pushes the palate down and the uvula across; parapharyngeal pushes the whole side wall in and bulges the neck out.

cards.q: What is the key investigation for a suspected parapharyngeal abscess, and what does it show?
cards.a:
• **Contrast-enhanced CT (CECT) of the neck** (extend to the chest if mediastinal spread suspected)
• Shows a **rim-enhancing fluid collection**, its compartment (pre- vs poststyloid) and relation to the **carotid sheath**
• Detects spread to retropharyngeal space or mediastinum and IJV thrombosis
• Plus: FBC, CRP, blood cultures, glucose; assess the **airway** first
cards.m: No CT, no knife – you must see the carotid before you drain.

cards.q: How is a parapharyngeal abscess treated?
cards.a:
• **Secure the airway** (stridor → awake fibreoptic intubation or tracheostomy)
• **IV antibiotics** covering aerobes and anaerobes (e.g. co-amoxiclav or ceftriaxone + metronidazole)
• **Incision and drainage – transcervical (external) approach** is standard for most, and for large or **poststyloid** abscesses: protects the great vessels
• **Transoral** drainage only for select, accessible abscesses medial to and away from the carotid/IJV
cards.m: Go in from the neck where you can see and control the carotid – not blindly through the mouth.

cards.q: What are the complications of a parapharyngeal abscess?
cards.a:
• **Acute laryngeal oedema** with respiratory obstruction
• **Thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein** with septicaemia (Lemierre syndrome)
• **Carotid artery erosion** – sentinel bleeding, haemorrhage
• Spread to the **retropharyngeal space**
• Spread to the **mediastinum** along the carotid sheath → mediastinitis
cards.m: Airway, Vessels, Spread – the three ways it kills.

cards.q: Why is acute retropharyngeal abscess mainly a disease of young children?
cards.a:
• The retropharyngeal space contains **retropharyngeal lymph nodes (nodes of Rouvière)** draining the nose, adenoids, nasopharynx and Eustachian tube
• These nodes **regress by about 3-5 years** of age
• Acute RPA = **suppuration of these nodes** after URTI, adenoiditis, tonsillitis or nasopharyngitis
• Hence most acute cases are in children **under 5**; in adults think trauma (fish bone, instrumentation) or TB
cards.m: No nodes, no acute abscess – Rouvière's nodes retire before school age.

cards.q: What are the clinical features of an acute retropharyngeal abscess?
cards.a:
• Young child, **sudden rapid progression** after a URTI; fever, irritability
• **Dysphagia**, **drooling**, refusal to feed
• **Difficulty breathing**, **stridor**, **croupy cough**
• **Neck held stiff / extended**, torticollis
• **Bulge of the posterior pharyngeal wall**, typically to **one side of the midline**
cards.m: A drooling child with stridor who will not move the neck – look behind the pharynx.

cards.q: Why is the bulge of an acute retropharyngeal abscess off the midline but a chronic one central?
cards.a:
• Acute: pus is in the **retropharyngeal space**, divided in the midline by a fibrous **median raphe** (superior constrictor attached to the fascia) → bulge on **one side**
• Chronic (TB of cervical spine): pus is **behind the prevertebral fascia**, which has no midline septum → **central** bulge
• Lateral X-ray in chronic cases may show vertebral body destruction
cards.m: Acute = Aside (one side); Chronic = Central.

cards.q: How is an acute retropharyngeal abscess investigated?
cards.a:
• **Airway first** – examine gently; do not upset a child with stridor
• **Lateral soft-tissue X-ray of the neck** (neck extended, on inspiration): **prevertebral widening** (more than about 7 mm at C2 or more than about half the vertebral body width), air-fluid level, loss of cervical lordosis
• **CECT neck** – confirms abscess vs cellulitis and shows extent (mediastinum)
• **FBC (raised WBC), ESR, CRP**, blood culture
cards.m: Lateral neck film in a child: prevertebral soft tissue at C2 thicker than about 7 mm = suspect pus.

cards.q: How is an acute retropharyngeal abscess managed?
cards.a:
• **Secure the airway** – may need intubation or **tracheostomy**
• **Intraoral incision and drainage** with the child in **Trendelenburg (head-down) position** and suction ready, to prevent aspiration of pus
• **IV antibiotics** (e.g. co-amoxiclav or ceftriaxone + metronidazole), IV fluids
• Small phlegmons may settle on antibiotics alone with close monitoring
cards.m: Head down, suck, cut – so the pus runs out of the mouth, not into the lungs.

cards.q: What are the features and management of a chronic retropharyngeal abscess?
cards.a:
• **Adult**; **slow, insidious** onset
• Cause: **TB** of retropharyngeal nodes (from deep cervical node TB) or **caries of the cervical spine (Pott's disease)** – actually in the prevertebral space
• Features: throat discomfort, mild dysphagia, **spinal tenderness**, **central fluctuant swelling** of the posterior pharyngeal wall
• Investigations: FBC, ESR, CRP, CT/MRI spine and neck, CXR, AFB/GeneXpert on pus
• Treatment: **antitubercular therapy**; drain **externally** (incision behind the sternocleidomastoid), not intraorally – avoids a chronic sinus
cards.m: Chronic = Cold abscess, Central bulge, Cervical spine TB, Cut from outside.

cards.q: What are the complications of a retropharyngeal abscess?
cards.a:
• **Airway obstruction** (oedema or spontaneous rupture and aspiration of pus)
• **Sepsis**
• **Mediastinitis** – via the danger space
• **Purulent meningitis**
• Others: IJV thrombosis, carotid erosion, atlanto-axial instability (Grisel syndrome)
cards.m: 'ASMM': Airway, Sepsis, Mediastinum, Meninges.

cards.q: How are oropharyngeal tumours classified, and what are the sites of malignancy?
cards.a:
• **Benign:** papilloma, haemangioma, pleomorphic adenoma (minor salivary glands), mucous cyst
• **Malignant sites:** **posterior 1/3 (base) of tongue**, **tonsil and tonsillar fossa**, **faucial arch** (anterior pillar / soft palate), **posterior and lateral pharyngeal wall**
• Note: slide p42 says 'posterior and lateral laryngeal arch'; correct is posterior and lateral **pharyngeal** wall
cards.m: Four malignant sites = Tongue base, Tonsil, Tonsillar pillar (faucial arch), back wall.

cards.q: What are the features and treatment of an oropharyngeal squamous papilloma?
cards.a:
• Caused by **HPV 6 and 11** (low-risk types)
• **Pedunculated**, pink or whitish, **cauliflower-like** lesion
• Arises from the **tonsil, soft palate, uvula or faucial pillars**
• Usually **asymptomatic**, found incidentally
• Treatment: **surgical excision** (send for histology)
cards.m: HPV 6 and 11 make warts; HPV 16 and 18 make cancer.

cards.q: When does an oropharyngeal haemangioma need treatment, and how is it treated?
cards.a:
• Sites: palate, tonsil, posterior and lateral **pharyngeal** wall
• Types: **capillary** or **cavernous**
• Treat if **increasing in size**, **bleeding** or causing **dysphagia**
• Options: **sclerotherapy**, **laser coagulation**, cryotherapy
• Never biopsy blindly – a bluish compressible lesion bleeds heavily
• Note: slide p43 says 'laryngeal wall'; correct is pharyngeal wall
cards.m: Blue, squashy, bleeds – laser or sclerose, never casually biopsy.

cards.q: Where do oropharyngeal mucous cysts arise, and how are they managed?
cards.a:
• Usually in the **vallecula** (between base of tongue and epiglottis)
• **Yellowish**, pedunculated or sessile; retention of mucus from a blocked minor gland
• Large ones cause dysphagia, foreign-body sensation or airway obstruction (infants)
• **Pedunculated → surgical excision**; **sessile → incision and drainage** (or marsupialisation)
cards.m: Vallecular cyst = yellow balloon in the valley.

cards.q: What are the key points about pleomorphic adenoma in the oropharynx?
cards.a:
• **Commonest benign salivary gland tumour** – most in the parotid
• In the oropharynx it arises from **minor salivary glands** of the **hard and soft palate** (or a parotid deep lobe presenting as a parapharyngeal mass)
• Painless, smooth, slow-growing, submucosal swelling
• **Potentially malignant** (carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma) and recurs if shelled out
• Treatment: **complete wide surgical excision** with a cuff; superficial/total parotidectomy for parotid lesions
cards.m: Pleomorphic = many faces, many recurrences – take a cuff, not a scoop.

cards.q: What are the aetiology and pathology of oropharyngeal carcinoma?
cards.a:
• Risk factors: **tobacco**, **alcohol** (synergistic), **HPV (especially HPV-16)**, immunosuppression, family history; betel quid chewing in South-East Asia
• Histology: **squamous cell carcinoma** (vast majority); also **lymphoma** (tonsil, base of tongue) and adenocarcinoma (minor salivary glands)
• Gross types: superficial spreading, **exophytic**, **ulcerative**, **infiltrative**
• Spread: local, **lymphatic (early, often bilateral)**, distant (lungs, bone)
cards.m: Smoke, drink, HPV-16 – SCC in nine out of ten.

cards.q: How does HPV-associated oropharyngeal carcinoma differ from tobacco-related disease?
cards.a:
• Driven by **HPV-16**; marker: **p16 immunohistochemistry positive**
• **Younger** patients, often **non-smokers** and non-drinkers
• Typically **tonsil or base of tongue**; small primary with a large **cystic neck node**
• **Much better prognosis** and response to (chemo)radiotherapy
• Staged separately in **AJCC 8th edition** (p16+ vs p16−)
• A cystic neck lump in an adult is **metastatic SCC until proven otherwise** – not a branchial cyst
cards.m: HPV-positive = Healthier, Happier Prognosis – young, non-smoker, cystic node.

cards.q: What is the T staging of (p16-negative) oropharyngeal carcinoma?
cards.a:
• **T1:** ≤ 2 cm
• **T2:** > 2 cm but ≤ 4 cm
• **T3:** > 4 cm, or extension to the **lingual surface of the epiglottis**
• **T4a:** invades **larynx**, **extrinsic tongue muscles**, **medial pterygoid**, **hard palate** or **mandible**
• **T4b:** lateral pterygoid, pterygoid plates, lateral nasopharynx, skull base or encasing the carotid
cards.m: 2-4-beyond: T1 up to 2, T2 up to 4, T3 over 4, T4 invades neighbours.

cards.q: How does carcinoma of the base (posterior 1/3) of the tongue present?
cards.a:
• **Initially silent** – the base of tongue is hidden and less sensitive
• Early: vague sore throat, mild odynophagia, **lump-in-throat** feeling
• Commonly first presents with a **neck lump** (nodal metastasis)
• Later: **referred otalgia** (CN IX), odynophagia, bleeding, **'hot potato' voice**, dysphagia, reduced tongue mobility
• Exophytic or infiltrating mass felt on **digital palpation**
cards.m: Base of tongue cancer whispers – neck lump and earache are often its first words.

cards.q: How do you diagnose and treat carcinoma of the base of tongue?
cards.a:
• Diagnosis: **palpation**, **laryngoscopy / flexible nasoendoscopy**, **CT/MRI** (local extent, nodes), **biopsy for HPE** (+ p16), CT thorax for staging
• Treatment: **radiotherapy** or **chemoradiotherapy** (organ-preserving)
• Or **surgery** (transoral robotic/laser resection, mandibulotomy approaches) + **neck dissection**
• Palliative: **tracheostomy**, **gastrostomy** feeding, analgesia
• Note: slide p47 says 'gastrotomy'; correct is gastrostomy
cards.m: Feel it, scope it, scan it, biopsy it – then radiate or resect.

cards.q: How does carcinoma of the tonsil present, and what should you do with a unilaterally enlarged tonsil in an adult?
cards.a:
• **Persistent unilateral sore throat**, odynophagia, **referred otalgia**, **neck lump**
• Progression: bleeding, **halitosis**, **trismus** (pterygoid invasion)
• Diagnosis: palpation (induration), **biopsy for HPE**, CT/MRI
• Treatment: radiotherapy / chemoradiotherapy, or surgery ± neck dissection
• **Unilateral tonsillar enlargement in an adult → excision biopsy (tonsillectomy)** to exclude **SCC or lymphoma**
cards.m: One big tonsil in an adult is a tumour until the pathologist says otherwise.

cards.q: How do carcinomas of the faucial arch and the posterior/lateral pharyngeal wall present and spread?
cards.a:
• **Faucial (palatine) arch:** persistent sore throat, local pain or earache, dysphagia; spreads to lymph nodes; diagnosis biopsy + CT; treatment irradiation or surgical excision
• **Posterior/lateral pharyngeal wall:** often **asymptomatic** until dysphagia; seen on indirect laryngoscopy/endoscopy
• Wall tumours spread **submucosally** to tonsil, soft palate, tongue, nasopharynx, hypopharynx; may invade the **parapharyngeal space** or **anterior spinal ligament**; early **node metastases** (retropharyngeal)
• Wall treatment: radiotherapy; surgical excision with skin grafting
cards.m: The back wall hides its spread under the mucosa – what you see is the tip of the iceberg.

cards.q: What are central, obstructive and mixed sleep apnoea?
cards.a:
• **Apnoea:** cessation of airflow for **≥ 10 seconds**; **hypopnoea:** ≥ 30% fall in airflow with ≥ 3% desaturation or arousal
• **Obstructive:** upper airway **collapses**; respiratory **effort continues** against the closed airway
• **Central:** airway patent but the **brain fails to signal** the respiratory muscles – **no effort**
• **Mixed:** begins central, ends obstructive
cards.m: Obstructive = trying but blocked; Central = not even trying.

cards.q: What are the anatomical risk factors for OSA?
cards.a:
• **Micrognathia / retrognathia**, **mandibular hypoplasia**
• **Facial elongation**
• **Adenotonsillar hypertrophy** – commonest cause in children
• **Inferior displacement of the hyoid**
• Also: macroglossia, nasal obstruction (septal deviation, polyps, turbinate hypertrophy), crowded oropharynx
cards.m: Small jaw, big tonsils, low hyoid = a small box with too much in it.

cards.q: What are the non-anatomical and medical risk factors for OSA?
cards.a:
• **Obesity** (central fat, large neck), **male sex**, **advancing age**, **supine sleeping**, **pregnancy**
• Medical: **hypothyroidism** and **acromegaly** (endocrine), **Down syndrome**, **Prader-Willi syndrome**, neuromuscular/neurological disease, **congestive heart failure**
• Others: **alcohol**, **sedatives and hypnotics**, **smoking**
cards.m: Fat, fifty, male, on his back after a few drinks – the classic snorer.

cards.q: Why does the upper airway collapse during sleep in OSA, and why is REM sleep worst?
cards.a:
• Sleep **reduces pharyngeal dilator muscle tone** → narrower, floppy airway → collapse in an anatomically narrow airway
• **REM sleep** → **greatest muscle relaxation (atonia)** → longest, deepest events
• **Alcohol and sedatives** further suppress muscle activity and arousal → more collapse
• Each event ends with an **arousal** that fragments sleep → daytime sleepiness
cards.m: Asleep, the throat is a wet paper straw – it collapses when the muscles holding it open switch off.

cards.q: What is 'high loop gain' and how does it worsen OSA?
cards.a:
• Loop gain = sensitivity of the **respiratory control system** to changes in CO2
• Obstruction → O2 falls, CO2 rises → over-sensitive brain responds with **rapid deep breathing**
• Overshoot blows off CO2 → **hypocapnia** → central drive falls → breathing **temporarily stops**
• Low drive also **reduces dilator muscle activity** → airway more likely to collapse → cycle repeats
cards.m: Like an over-sensitive thermostat: overshoots, undershoots, never settles.

cards.q: What are the night-time features of OSA?
cards.a:
• **Loud habitual snoring**
• **Witnessed apnoeas** (pauses noticed by the bed partner)
• **Gasping or choking** on waking
• **Nocturia**
• Restless sleep, night sweats
• Children: snoring, mouth breathing, restless sleep, enuresis
cards.m: The bed partner gives the history – ask them.

cards.q: What are the daytime features of OSA?
cards.a:
• **Excessive daytime sleepiness** (falling asleep driving, in meetings)
• **Morning headache** (CO2 retention), fatigue
• **Dry mouth or sore throat** on waking
• Poor concentration, **memory problems**, forgetfulness
• **Mood changes** (irritability, depression), reduced libido
• Children: hyperactivity, behavioural problems, poor school performance, failure to thrive
cards.m: Sleepy adults, hyperactive children.

cards.q: What should you look for on examination of a patient with suspected OSA?
cards.a:
• **General:** BMI (obesity), **neck circumference > 40 cm** (> 43 cm men, > 40 cm women in some texts), **blood pressure**
• **Craniofacial:** **micrognathia / retrognathia**, high-arched palate
• **Oropharynx:** crowded oropharynx, **modified Mallampati grade 3-4**, **enlarged tonsils**, macroglossia, long soft palate/uvula
• **Nose:** septal deviation, turbinate hypertrophy, polyps
• Note: slide p55 says 'Anthropometic'; the term is anthropometric
cards.m: Weigh, measure the neck, look at the jaw, look in the mouth, look up the nose.

cards.q: What is the STOP-BANG questionnaire and how is it interpreted?
cards.a:
• **S**noring, **T**iredness, **O**bserved apnoea, high blood **P**ressure
• **B**MI > 35 kg/m², **A**ge > 50 years, **N**eck > 40 cm, male **G**ender
• 1 point each (0-8): **0-2 low**, **3-4 intermediate**, **5-8 high risk**
• **Score ≥ 3 = increased risk → refer for a sleep study**
• Screening tool only – it does not diagnose OSA
• Note: slide p56 writes 'STOP-BANG > 3'; standard cut-off is ≥ 3
cards.m: Three ticks and you are in the sleep lab.

cards.q: What is the Epworth Sleepiness Scale and what does it tell you?
cards.a:
• Self-rated chance of dozing in **8 everyday situations**, each scored **0-3** → total **0-24**
• **> 10 = excessive daytime sleepiness**
• Measures **subjective sleepiness only** – **not diagnostic** of OSA (many patients with severe OSA score low)
• Useful to track response to treatment and for driving assessment
cards.m: Eight situations × three points = 24; double figures (> 10) = sleepy.

cards.q: What are the four levels of sleep study, and which can diagnose OSA?
cards.a:
• **Level 1:** full **attended in-lab PSG** (≥ 7 channels, staff present) – gold standard
• **Level 2:** full **unattended PSG** (≥ 7 channels)
• **Level 3:** portable / home sleep apnoea test (**HSAT**, ≥ 4 channels)
• **Level 4:** 1-2 channels (e.g. **overnight oximetry**) – **screening only**
• OSA is diagnosed with **level 1, 2 or 3**
• Negative, inconclusive or inadequate HSAT despite high suspicion → **full PSG**
cards.m: Levels 1-3 diagnose; level 4 only knocks on the door.

cards.q: What is the AHI, what are the adult diagnostic criteria for OSA, and how is severity graded?
cards.a:
• **AHI = (apnoeas + hypopnoeas) per hour of sleep**
• Diagnosis: **AHI ≥ 5** with typical symptoms or associated disease (hypertension, IHD, stroke, AF), **or AHI ≥ 15** even without symptoms
• Severity: **mild 5 to < 15**, **moderate 15-30**, **severe > 30** events/h
• Children: **AHI > 1** is abnormal
cards.m: 5-15-30: the three doors of OSA severity.

cards.q: How is the site of upper-airway obstruction assessed before OSA surgery?
cards.a:
• **Drug-induced sleep endoscopy (DISE):** flexible endoscopy under sedation (e.g. propofol) that mimics sleep; shows the **site, degree and pattern** of dynamic collapse (velum, oropharynx, tongue base, epiglottis)
• Malaysian CPG: DISE is **more accurate** than awake assessment for planning sleep surgery
• **Fibre-optic nasendoscopy with Müller manoeuvre (FNMM):** awake; patient inspires forcibly against a closed mouth and nose; identifies level of collapse
• FNMM may be offered when **DISE cannot be performed**
cards.m: DISE watches the airway asleep; Müller asks the awake patient to pretend.

cards.q: What are the main differential diagnoses of OSA?
cards.a:
• **Central sleep apnoea:** apnoea **without respiratory effort**; heart failure (Cheyne-Stokes), stroke, **opioids**, neurological disease
• **Obesity hypoventilation syndrome:** **BMI ≥ 30 + awake PaCO2 > 45 mmHg**, other causes excluded
• **Primary snoring:** loud snoring but **no witnessed apnoea, desaturation or significant daytime sleepiness**
• Upper airway obstruction (nasal, adenotonsillar) and **insomnia** (fatigue without apnoeas)
• Others: narcolepsy, depression, hypothyroidism, shift work
cards.m: No effort = central; high CO2 awake = OHS; noise only = primary snoring.

cards.q: What are the conservative (lifestyle and positional) measures for OSA?
cards.a:
• **Weight reduction** – diet, exercise; bariatric surgery for morbid obesity
• **Avoid alcohol, sedatives and smoking** (especially in the evening)
• **Positional therapy:** sleep on the side; **tennis-ball technique** (ball sewn into the back of the pyjamas) prevents supine sleep
• Treat nasal disease: **intranasal corticosteroids** for allergic rhinitis / chronic rhinosinusitis
• Sleep hygiene; treat hypothyroidism if present
cards.m: Lose weight, lose the nightcap, lose the back position.

cards.q: What is CPAP, and what is its role in OSA?
cards.a:
• **Continuous positive airway pressure** via nasal or full-face mask acts as a **pneumatic splint** holding the pharynx open
• **First-line / gold-standard treatment for moderate-severe OSA** and symptomatic mild OSA
• Improves sleepiness, BP, quality of life and driving safety
• Main problem: **adherence** (mask discomfort, nasal blockage, claustrophobia)
• **BiPAP** (separate inspiratory and expiratory pressures) for CPAP intolerance at high pressures or coexisting hypoventilation (OHS, COPD)
cards.m: CPAP = an air splint – it blows the floppy throat open.

cards.q: What intraoral devices are used for OSA, and for whom?
cards.a:
• **Mandibular advancement appliance (MAA/MAD):** holds the lower jaw forward → pulls the tongue base forward, enlarges the airway
• **Tongue-retaining device (TRD):** suction bulb holds the tongue forward (edentulous patients)
• Indicated for **mild-moderate OSA**, primary snoring, or **CPAP-intolerant** patients
• Need adequate healthy teeth; side effects: jaw/TMJ pain, tooth movement
cards.m: Jaw forward, tongue forward, airway open.

cards.q: What is the role of nasal surgery in OSA?
cards.a:
• Procedures: **septoplasty**, **inferior turbinate reduction**, **polypectomy** / FESS
• Reduces nasal resistance and mouth breathing
• Rarely cures OSA alone – mainly **improves CPAP tolerance** (lower pressure, better mask comfort) and snoring
• Combine with intranasal steroids for allergic or inflammatory disease
cards.m: Fix the nose to help the mask, not to replace it.

cards.q: What soft-tissue (pharyngeal) operations are used for OSA?
cards.a:
• **Tonsillectomy ± adenoidectomy** – very effective when tonsils are large
• **Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty (UPPP):** removes uvula, redundant soft palate and tonsils, tightens pillars
• **Expansion / reposition pharyngoplasty** and **uvulopalatoplasty** (e.g. laser-assisted, mainly for snoring) – separate procedures
• **Tongue base radiofrequency reduction**
• Best chosen after **DISE** shows the level of collapse
• Note: slide p61 lists uvulopalatoplasty as if it were a type of reposition pharyngoplasty; they are different operations
cards.m: Soft-tissue surgery trims the curtains (palate, uvula, tonsils, tongue base).

cards.q: What skeletal surgery is used for OSA, and what is the last-resort operation?
cards.a:
• **Genioplasty (genioglossus advancement) with hyoid suspension** – pulls the tongue base and hyoid forward
• **Maxillomandibular osteotomy and advancement (MMA)** – moves both jaws forward; most effective surgery for severe OSA / retrognathia
• **Tracheostomy** – bypasses all upper-airway obstruction; **last resort** for severe OSA failing other treatment (e.g. cor pulmonale, life-threatening hypoxia)
cards.m: Soft tissue trims the curtains; skeletal surgery moves the window frame; tracheostomy builds a new door.

cards.q: What is the first-line treatment of OSA in children?
cards.a:
• Commonest cause: **adenotonsillar hypertrophy**
• **Adenotonsillectomy** is first-line in otherwise healthy children
• Monitor overnight post-op if severe OSA, age < 3 years, obesity, Down syndrome, craniofacial or neuromuscular disease (airway complications)
• Persistent OSA after surgery (obese, syndromic) → **CPAP**
• Mild cases: intranasal steroids / montelukast may help
cards.m: In children, take out the tonsils and adenoids before you reach for the mask.

cards.q: What are the cardiovascular complications of untreated OSA?
cards.a:
• **Systemic hypertension** – classically **resistant hypertension**
• **Atrial and ventricular arrhythmias** (especially **atrial fibrillation**)
• **Angina / ischaemic heart disease**
• **Congestive heart failure** and **pulmonary hypertension / cor pulmonale**
• **Stroke**
• Mechanism: repeated hypoxia and arousals → sympathetic surges, oxidative stress, intrathoracic pressure swings
cards.m: OSA strains the heart every night – hundreds of tiny suffocations.

cards.q: What are the non-cardiac complications of OSA, and what driving advice should you give?
cards.a:
• **Road traffic accidents** from sleepiness
• **Snoring spouse syndrome** – partner's sleep disturbed
• **Loss of memory**, poor concentration, depression
• **Decreased libido**, erectile dysfunction
• Metabolic: insulin resistance / diabetes
• Driving: advise **not to drive while sleepy**; resume once symptoms are controlled on treatment (e.g. CPAP); inform the licensing authority if required, especially commercial drivers
cards.m: Sleepy at the wheel kills – treat first, drive later.

mcq.stem:
A 26-year-old woman attends the ENT clinic two days after an elective tonsillectomy. She complains of severe right earache, worse on swallowing. Otoscopy shows normal, mobile tympanic membranes and she is afebrile.
Which nerve is most likely carrying this pain to the ear?
o: Auricular branch of the vagus nerve (Arnold's nerve)
Auriculotemporal branch of the mandibular nerve
Tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve
Great auricular nerve from the C2-C3 roots
Lesser occipital nerve from the C2 root
mcq.e: The tonsil and tonsillar bed are supplied by the **glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)**, whose **tympanic (Jacobson's) branch** also supplies the middle ear mucosa, so tonsil-bed pain is felt in the ear. This is why referred otalgia follows tonsillectomy, tonsillitis and quinsy with a normal drum. Arnold's nerve (X) is the pathway for otalgia from laryngeal and hypopharyngeal lesions.
w: Wrong - Arnold's nerve refers pain from the larynx and hypopharynx (vagal territory), not from the tonsil bed.
Wrong - the auriculotemporal nerve refers pain from the teeth, TMJ and anterior tongue, not the tonsillar fossa.
Correct - CN IX supplies the tonsil bed and, via Jacobson's nerve, the tympanic cavity.
Wrong - C2-C3 refer pain from the cervical spine and neck, not from the oropharynx.
Wrong - the lesser occipital nerve supplies skin behind the ear and carries no oropharyngeal sensation.

mcq.stem:
A 58-year-old man is reviewed in the ENT clinic after resection of a left jugular foramen tumour. His voice is hoarse and breathy. On saying 'Ah', the uvula is pulled to the right; the tongue protrudes in the midline and facial sensation is intact.
Which nerve lesion best explains the palatal findings?
o: Left vagus nerve via the pharyngeal plexus
Right vagus nerve via the pharyngeal plexus
Left mandibular nerve to tensor veli palatini
Right glossopharyngeal nerve
Left hypoglossal nerve
mcq.e: All soft palate muscles except **tensor veli palatini (V3)** are supplied by the **vagus via the pharyngeal plexus**. When one side is paralysed, the intact levator veli palatini pulls the uvula **towards the healthy side**, so a uvula pulled to the right means a **left** vagal lesion, fitting a left jugular foramen tumour. Tensor veli palatini is too weak to deviate the uvula on its own.
w: Correct - left X palsy: the intact right levator veli palatini pulls the uvula to the right.
Wrong - a right vagal lesion would pull the uvula to the left, towards the healthy side.
Wrong - loss of tensor veli palatini (V3) does not visibly deviate the uvula, and facial sensation is intact.
Wrong - CN IX is mainly sensory to the oropharynx (gag afferent); it does not elevate the palate.
Wrong - a XII palsy causes tongue deviation on protrusion, which is absent here.

mcq.stem:
A 17-year-old boy presents to the Klinik Kesihatan with 3 days of fever and painful swallowing. Both tonsils are red and swollen. A single tender, enlarged lymph node is palpable just below and behind the angle of the mandible, deep to the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid.
Which lymph node is this?
o: Retropharyngeal node of Rouvière (lateral group)
Submental node of the superficial ring
Jugulo-omohyoid node of the lower deep chain
Pre-auricular node of the parotid group
Jugulodigastric node of the upper deep chain
mcq.e: The palatine tonsil drains mainly to the **jugulodigastric node** (the 'tonsillar node') of the upper deep cervical chain, which enlarges and becomes tender in tonsillitis and may suppurate into a cervical abscess. Note: slide p11 lists only retropharyngeal nodes; these receive some pharyngeal drainage but are impalpable and regress in early childhood. Correct is the jugulodigastric node as the main tonsillar node, as slide p22 states.
w: Wrong - retropharyngeal nodes lie behind the pharynx, cannot be palpated in the neck and regress by about 3-5 years.
Wrong - submental nodes drain the chin, lower lip and tip of the tongue.
Wrong - the jugulo-omohyoid node lies low, where omohyoid crosses the IJV, and is the key node for the tongue.
Wrong - pre-auricular nodes drain the scalp, eyelids and parotid region.
Correct - the jugulodigastric (tonsillar) node is the main drainage of the palatine tonsil.

mcq.stem:
A 64-year-old man is seen on the surgical ward after a right carotid endarterectomy. On protrusion his tongue deviates to the right and the right half shows early fasciculation. Palatal movement and the gag reflex are normal.
Which muscle acting on the tongue is NOT supplied by the injured nerve?
o: Genioglossus
Palatoglossus
Hyoglossus
Styloglossus
Superior longitudinal (intrinsic)
mcq.e: The injured nerve is the **hypoglossal (XII)**, which supplies all intrinsic and extrinsic tongue muscles **except palatoglossus**, supplied by the **vagus via the pharyngeal plexus** (it is really a palatal muscle and forms the anterior tonsillar pillar). The tongue deviates towards the side of a LMN XII lesion because the healthy genioglossus pushes it across.
w: Wrong - genioglossus is supplied by XII; its weakness is why the tongue deviates to the lesion side.
Correct - palatoglossus is supplied by X via the pharyngeal plexus and forms the anterior pillar.
Wrong - hyoglossus is supplied by XII.
Wrong - styloglossus is supplied by XII.
Wrong - all intrinsic tongue muscles are supplied by XII.

mcq.stem:
A 6-year-old unvaccinated girl is reviewed on the paediatric ward three weeks after a severe throat infection. Her mother reports that milk comes out of her nose when she drinks, and her speech has become nasal. The pharynx now looks clear.
Failure of which pharyngeal-phase event best explains the nasal regurgitation?
o: Elevation of the larynx under the base of the tongue
Backward folding of the epiglottis over the inlet
Adduction of the vocal cords during swallowing apnoea
Elevation of the soft palate to seal the nasopharynx
Relaxation of the upper oesophageal sphincter
mcq.e: In the **pharyngeal (involuntary) phase** the soft palate rises against the posterior pharyngeal wall to **close the nasopharyngeal isthmus**, so the bolus cannot enter the nose. Palatal paralysis, classically post-diphtheritic 2-3 weeks after the throat infection, causes nasal regurgitation and hypernasal speech. Laryngeal elevation, epiglottic folding and cord closure protect the lower airway; their failure causes aspiration and coughing, not nasal reflux.
w: Wrong - poor laryngeal elevation leads to aspiration into the larynx, not fluid from the nose.
Wrong - epiglottic failure lets the bolus enter the laryngeal inlet (aspiration).
Wrong - cord closure (deglutition apnoea) protects the trachea; failure causes coughing and choking.
Correct - the soft palate must close the nasopharynx; palatal palsy gives nasal regurgitation and nasal speech.
Wrong - failure of UES relaxation causes pooling in the pyriform fossae and overflow aspiration.

mcq.stem:
A mother in the ENT clinic asks how her 5-year-old son's tonsils 'fight germs' before agreeing to tonsillectomy for recurrent tonsillitis. You explain how antigens in the tonsillar crypts reach the lymphoid tissue and which antibody guards the mucosal surface.
Which pairing is correct?
o: M (microfold) cells and secretory IgA
Goblet cells and secretory IgA
M (microfold) cells and IgE
Langerhans cells and IgG
Follicular dendritic cells and secretory IgA
mcq.e: **M (microfold) cells** overlying the tonsillar crypts capture antigens and deliver them to the underlying lymphoid follicles, activating T and B lymphocytes. B cells produce **secretory IgA** for mucosal protection, while IgG and IgM neutralise organisms and T cells provide cell-mediated immunity. Removing the tonsils causes no clinically important immune deficit because the rest of the mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue compensates.
w: Correct - M cells sample crypt antigens; B cells make secretory IgA for mucosal defence.
Wrong - goblet cells secrete mucus and do not transport antigen, although IgA is right.
Wrong - IgE mediates allergy and antiparasitic defence, not routine mucosal protection.
Wrong - Langerhans cells belong to squamous surface epithelium and IgG acts mainly in serum and tissues.
Wrong - follicular dendritic cells sit in germinal centres presenting antigen to B cells; they do not sample the crypt lumen.

mcq.stem:
A 19-year-old university student presents to the Klinik Kesihatan with a 6-day sore throat, fever and marked fatigue. Both tonsils are enlarged with a creamy exudate. There are palatal petechiae, tender posterior cervical and axillary nodes and a palpable spleen tip. A widespread itchy maculopapular rash appeared two days after starting amoxicillin.
Which investigation is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
o: Throat swab for group A streptococcal culture
Antistreptolysin O titre at presentation
Monospot test with a peripheral blood film
Swab culture on Loeffler's serum medium
Skin patch testing for penicillin allergy
mcq.e: Generalised lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, palatal petechiae and an **amoxicillin rash** in a young adult point to **infectious mononucleosis (EBV)**. Confirm with a **Monospot (heterophile antibody)** test and a film showing **atypical lymphocytes**, with EBV serology if the Monospot is negative early. The rash is not a true penicillin allergy; advise avoiding contact sports for several weeks because of the risk of splenic rupture.
w: Wrong - a positive culture may only reflect carriage and does not explain splenomegaly and the drug rash.
Wrong - ASO rises late and shows past streptococcal infection, not the cause of this illness.
Correct - Monospot plus atypical lymphocytes on the film confirms EBV glandular fever.
Wrong - Loeffler's medium is for diphtheria, which gives an adherent grey membrane in the unvaccinated, not splenomegaly with a drug rash.
Wrong - the amoxicillin rash of EBV is not allergic; patch testing does not make the diagnosis.

mcq.stem:
A 5-year-old boy whose parents declined childhood vaccination is brought to the Emergency Department with 2 days of low-grade fever, sore throat and noisy breathing. He looks toxic, with marked soft-tissue swelling of the neck. A dirty grey membrane covers both tonsils and extends onto the uvula and soft palate; it bleeds when touched with a swab.
While securing the airway as needed, what is the most appropriate immediate management?
o: Oral penicillin V for 10 days and review in clinic
IV amoxicillin with a Monospot test before treating
Emergency tonsillectomy to remove the membrane
Metronidazole and chlorhexidine mouthwash
Isolate, give antitoxin and penicillin, and notify
mcq.e: An adherent grey membrane spreading **beyond the tonsil onto the uvula and palate** that **bleeds on removal**, with **bull neck** and toxicity in an unvaccinated child, is **diphtheria**. Give **diphtheria antitoxin** on clinical suspicion without waiting for culture, plus penicillin or erythromycin; isolate, protect the airway and **notify** (notifiable disease in Malaysia), and give contacts prophylaxis. The toxin causes myocarditis and palatal and cranial nerve palsies, so monitor the ECG.
w: Wrong - outpatient antibiotics alone leave circulating toxin untreated and skip isolation and notification.
Wrong - amoxicillin and Monospot target EBV; delaying antitoxin for tests worsens toxin damage.
Wrong - stripping or excising the membrane causes bleeding and toxin absorption; surgery has no acute role.
Wrong - metronidazole and mouthwash treat Vincent's angina, not a toxin-producing infection.
Correct - antitoxin early, antibiotics, isolation and notification are the core of diphtheria care.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old man who smokes heavily presents to the ENT clinic with a week of painful swallowing on the right and a foul taste. His gums are inflamed and bleed easily, with poor dental hygiene. The right tonsil has a punched-out ulcer covered by a yellow-grey slough that comes away easily; the left tonsil is normal. He is mildly febrile.
What would a Gram-stained smear from the ulcer most likely show?
o: Gram-positive cocci in long chains
Fusiform bacilli with numerous spirochaetes
Club-shaped Gram-positive rods in palisades
Pseudohyphae with budding yeast cells
Gram-negative intracellular diplococci
mcq.e: A unilateral ulcer with slough in a patient with **poor oral hygiene and gingivitis** is **Vincent's angina** (ulceromembranous tonsillitis), caused by **fusiform bacilli and spirochaetes** (Borrelia vincentii). Treat with penicillin or **metronidazole**, dental care and chlorhexidine or hydrogen peroxide mouthwash. In a smoker, a unilateral ulcer that has not healed within 2-3 weeks needs biopsy to exclude carcinoma.
w: Wrong - chains of cocci suggest streptococcal tonsillitis, which is usually bilateral and lacks gingivitis.
Correct - fusiform bacilli plus spirochaetes are the organisms of Vincent's angina.
Wrong - club-shaped palisading rods are Corynebacterium diphtheriae, which forms an adherent membrane that bleeds.
Wrong - Candida gives white plaques, mainly in the immunocompromised or after antibiotics or inhaled steroids.
Wrong - Gram-negative diplococci suggest gonococcal pharyngitis, which does not cause a punched-out ulcer with gingivitis.

mcq.stem:
Five children aged 5-10 years are referred from Klinik Kesihatan to the ENT clinic for recurrent sore throats. Every episode was documented with fever above 38.3 °C, tonsillar exudate or tender cervical nodes, and antibiotic treatment.
Which child meets the frequency criteria for tonsillectomy?
o: Six episodes in the past 12 months, none before that
Four episodes a year in each of the last 2 years
Two episodes a year in each of the last 4 years
Three episodes a year in each of the last 3 years
Five episodes this year and two the year before
mcq.e: The **Paradise criteria** for recurrent tonsillitis are **≥ 7 episodes in 1 year, ≥ 5 a year for 2 years, or ≥ 3 a year for 3 years**, each episode documented (fever > 38.3 °C, exudate, tender nodes or positive streptococcal culture). Only three a year sustained over 3 years qualifies here. The other children can be watched, as many improve with age.
w: Wrong - six in one year falls short of the seven needed for the 1-year criterion.
Wrong - the 2-year criterion needs at least five episodes in each year.
Wrong - two a year meets no criterion, however long it continues.
Correct - at least three a year for 3 years meets the Paradise criteria.
Wrong - the earlier year has only two episodes, so neither the 1-year nor the 2-year criterion is met.

mcq.stem:
A 7-year-old boy with no drug allergies is seen at the Klinik Kesihatan with 2 days of fever of 39 °C, painful swallowing and no cough. The tonsils are swollen with exudate and the jugulodigastric nodes are tender. His mother asks what to give for the pain and fever.
Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Penicillin V for 10 days with paracetamol
Penicillin V for 10 days with aspirin
Amoxicillin for 5 days with aspirin
Erythromycin for 3 days with ibuprofen
Ciprofloxacin for 7 days with paracetamol
mcq.e: Probable bacterial tonsillitis (high Centor or FeverPAIN score) is treated with **penicillin V for 10 days**, the course needed to eradicate group A streptococcus and prevent rheumatic fever, with **paracetamol ± ibuprofen**, fluids and rest. **Avoid aspirin** in children (Reye syndrome) and in anyone who may need tonsil surgery (bleeding). Note: slide p28 says 'aspirin or paracetamol'; correct is paracetamol ± NSAID, never aspirin in a child. Macrolides are for penicillin allergy, and amoxicillin is avoided when glandular fever is possible.
w: Correct - 10 days of penicillin V with paracetamol is standard for streptococcal tonsillitis.
Wrong - aspirin is contraindicated under 16 years (Reye syndrome), even though the slide lists it.
Wrong - amoxicillin causes a rash if this is EBV, 5 days is too short, and aspirin is unsafe.
Wrong - erythromycin is for penicillin allergy, and 3 days will not eradicate the streptococcus.
Wrong - ciprofloxacin has poor streptococcal cover and is not used for tonsillitis in children.

mcq.stem:
A 42-year-old woman started carbimazole for Graves' disease 6 weeks ago. She presents to the Emergency Department with 2 days of high fever, rigors and a severe sore throat. Both tonsils show grey necrotic ulcers with dirty slough, but there is little cervical lymphadenopathy.
What is the most important next step?
o: Throat swab and start oral penicillin V
Monospot test and avoid contact sports
Urgent full blood count with differential
Diphtheria antitoxin and notify the outbreak
Excision biopsy of the more ulcerated tonsil
mcq.e: Necrotic tonsillar ulceration with fever and **little nodal response** in a patient on **carbimazole** suggests **drug-induced agranulocytosis**. Do an **urgent FBC with differential**; if neutrophils are low, stop carbimazole and treat as **neutropenic sepsis** with broad-spectrum IV antibiotics. Any tonsillar membrane in an unwell patient deserves an FBC to exclude agranulocytosis and leukaemia.
w: Wrong - oral penicillin as an outpatient is dangerous if she is neutropenic.
Wrong - EBV is unlikely at 42 on carbimazole, and the test ignores the life-threatening possibility.
Correct - the FBC confirms agranulocytosis, and the drug must be stopped at once.
Wrong - nothing suggests diphtheria (no adherent palatal membrane, no bull neck); antitoxin is not indicated.
Wrong - biopsy is for a unilateral suspicious lesion; bilateral necrosis with fever needs a blood count first.

mcq.stem:
A 10-year-old girl is seen at the Klinik Kesihatan with 1 day of fever, sore throat and pain on swallowing. Both tonsils are congested and studded with discrete yellowish spots of pus at the openings of the crypts; the spots have not joined into a sheet.
Which type of acute tonsillitis is this?
o: Catarrhal (superficial)
Follicular
Parenchymatous
Membranous
Chronic parenchymatous
mcq.e: In **follicular** tonsillitis the infection spreads into the **crypts**, which fill with pus seen as **discrete yellow spots** at their openings. When the crypt exudate **coalesces** into a continuous whitish sheet that wipes off easily, it is **membranous**. Catarrhal is superficial (often viral pharyngitis) and parenchymatous is uniform gross enlargement that may meet in the midline.
w: Wrong - catarrhal tonsillitis is limited to the surface epithelium with generalised pharyngitis, without crypt pus.
Correct - discrete pus spots at the crypt openings define follicular tonsillitis.
Wrong - parenchymatous means uniform enlargement of the whole tonsil, often meeting in the midline.
Wrong - membranous tonsillitis needs the crypt exudate to coalesce into a continuous membrane.
Wrong - this is a 1-day illness; chronic tonsillitis means symptoms lasting over 3 months.

mcq.stem:
A 23-year-old man attends the ENT clinic with a year of recurrent sore throats, a persistent bad taste and halitosis noticed by his family. Between attacks he is well. The tonsils are small, but pressing on the anterior pillar squeezes out cheesy material; the anterior pillars are flushed compared with the rest of the pharynx and the jugulodigastric nodes are palpable.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Tonsillar retention cyst
Isolated tonsillolith
Vincent's angina
Carcinoma of the tonsil
Chronic tonsillitis
mcq.e: Recurrent sore throats, halitosis and bad taste with **cheesy material expressed from the crypts**, **flushed anterior pillars** and **enlarged jugulodigastric nodes** indicate **chronic tonsillitis**; small tonsils fit the fibroid type, so size is not the test. Treat coexisting dental or sinus infection and offer tonsillectomy if attacks recur or symptoms interfere with life.
w: Wrong - a retention cyst is a smooth yellowish swelling, usually symptomless, without flushed pillars or nodes.
Wrong - a tonsillolith is a hard calcified stone in one crypt, not diffuse cheesy debris with inflamed pillars.
Wrong - Vincent's angina is an acute ulcer with slough and gingivitis.
Wrong - carcinoma is usually a unilateral ulcer or enlargement with progressive pain in an older smoker.
Correct - crypt debris, flushed anterior pillars and nodes are the signs of chronic tonsillitis.

mcq.stem:
A 6-year-old boy is on the ENT ward 4 hours after tonsillectomy. The nurse notes he is swallowing repeatedly, his pulse has risen from 100 to 140/min and he has vomited dark blood. Fresh clot is seen in the left tonsillar fossa; capillary refill time is 3 seconds.
After starting resuscitation, what is the most appropriate next step?
o: Observe on the ward with hourly pulse charting
Oral antibiotics and hydrogen peroxide gargles
Remove the clot and apply pressure with the child awake
Return to theatre under GA to secure the bleeding
Admit for IV antibiotics and review in 24 hours
mcq.e: Bleeding within **24 hours** (usually the first few hours) is **primary or reactionary haemorrhage**, from a slipped tie or a vessel opening up as blood pressure recovers after anaesthesia. Repeated swallowing with tachycardia in a child means a large loss from a small circulating volume. Resuscitate (IV access, cross-match, fluids or blood) and **return to theatre** promptly to secure the vessel, with a senior anaesthetist because of the full stomach and blood in the airway.
w: Wrong - tachycardia and repeated swallowing mean significant blood loss; watching delays definitive control.
Wrong - antibiotics and gargles are for secondary (infective) haemorrhage at day 5-10, not a bleed at 4 hours.
Wrong - an awake child will not tolerate clot removal or pressure, and it risks aspiration.
Correct - reactionary haemorrhage with haemodynamic change needs haemostasis in theatre.
Wrong - this is the plan for secondary haemorrhage; reactionary bleeding is a mechanical problem.

mcq.stem:
A 24-year-old woman returns to the Emergency Department on day 7 after tonsillectomy with a small amount of fresh bleeding from the mouth. She has had worsening throat pain and a temperature of 38.2 °C. The tonsillar fossae are covered with thick, foul-smelling slough, and the oozing has now stopped.
What is the most likely underlying cause of this bleed?
o: Infection of the healing tonsil bed
Slipped ligature on a tonsillar vessel
Undiagnosed von Willebrand disease
Erosion of the internal carotid artery
Rebound rise in blood pressure after GA
mcq.e: Bleeding between **day 5 and 10** is **secondary haemorrhage**, caused by **infection** of the tonsillar fossa as slough separates from the raw bed. Admit, establish IV access, give **IV antibiotics** and send a group and save; most settle, but persistent or heavy bleeding needs theatre.
