Slipped ties and the post-anaesthetic rise in blood pressure cause reactionary bleeding within 24 hours.
w: Correct - day 5-10 bleeding with fever and slough is infective secondary haemorrhage.
Wrong - a slipped tie bleeds within the first 24 hours (reactionary haemorrhage).
Wrong - a coagulopathy usually shows at or soon after surgery; fever and slough point to infection.
Wrong - carotid erosion is very rare and causes torrential bleeding, not a self-limiting ooze.
Wrong - blood pressure rebound after anaesthesia causes reactionary bleeding in the first hours.

mcq.stem:
Five patients on the ENT clinic list are asking about tonsillectomy. All are otherwise fit, with normal clotting and no current infection.
Which patient has an ABSOLUTE indication for tonsillectomy?
o: A 20-year-old man who is a symptomless diphtheria carrier
A 17-year-old girl with chronic tonsillitis and halitosis
A 4-year-old boy with tonsils causing OSA and poor growth
A 25-year-old nurse who is a group A streptococcal carrier
A 40-year-old with valvular disease and recurrent strep throat
mcq.e: **Obstructive tonsillar hypertrophy** causing sleep apnoea, failure to thrive or cor pulmonale is an **absolute** indication, alongside recurrent infection meeting the Paradise criteria, quinsy, tonsillitis causing febrile seizures and suspected malignancy. Carrier states (diphtheria, streptococcus), chronic tonsillitis with halitosis and recurrent streptococcal tonsillitis in valvular heart disease are **relative** indications, where surgery is reasonable but not mandatory.
w: Wrong - diphtheria carriage is a relative indication, usually treated first with antibiotics.
Wrong - chronic tonsillitis with halitosis is a relative indication.
Correct - airway obstruction with OSA and failure to thrive is an absolute indication.
Wrong - streptococcal carriage is a relative indication.
Wrong - recurrent streptococcal tonsillitis in valvular heart disease is a relative indication (endocarditis risk).

mcq.stem:
An 8-year-old girl is admitted on the morning of her elective tonsillectomy for recurrent tonsillitis. Since yesterday she has had a fever of 38.5 °C and a sore throat, and both tonsils are inflamed with exudate. Her haemoglobin and clotting screen are normal.
What is the most appropriate plan?
o: Proceed today under intravenous antibiotic cover
Postpone surgery for about 2-3 weeks after recovery
Proceed today as a hot tonsillectomy without antibiotics
Postpone for 6 months and recount the episodes
Cancel, as acute tonsillitis removes the indication
mcq.e: **Acute infection is a contraindication** to elective tonsillectomy: inflamed tissue bleeds more and the risk of secondary haemorrhage rises. Treat the attack and reschedule about **2-3 weeks** after it settles. Other contraindications include bleeding disorders, anaemia, cleft palate or submucous cleft and uncontrolled systemic disease.
w: Wrong - antibiotic cover does not remove the extra bleeding risk of operating through acute inflammation.
Correct - wait 2-3 weeks after the infection has settled, then operate.
Wrong - hot tonsillectomy is reserved for selected quinsy cases, not elective surgery during acute tonsillitis.
Wrong - a 6-month delay is unnecessary once the acute attack has resolved.
Wrong - this attack is further evidence of recurrent tonsillitis; the indication stands.

mcq.stem:
A 28-year-old man who smokes presents to the Emergency Department with 5 days of worsening left-sided sore throat, drooling and a muffled voice. He can open his mouth only 1.5 cm. The left soft palate and anterior pillar bulge above the tonsil and the uvula is pushed to the right.
Where is the pus most likely to be located?
o: Within the substance of the left palatine tonsil
Retropharyngeal space between buccopharyngeal and alar fascia
Parapharyngeal space lateral to the superior constrictor
Submandibular space below the mylohyoid muscle
Between the tonsil capsule and the superior constrictor
mcq.e: A unilateral bulge of the soft palate and anterior pillar **above the tonsil**, uvula pushed to the **opposite side**, trismus and hot potato voice is a **peritonsillar abscess (quinsy)**: pus in the **peritonsillar space between the tonsil capsule and the superior constrictor**. It usually follows tonsillitis, an intratonsillar abscess bursting through the capsule. Pus lateral to the constrictor (parapharyngeal) pushes the whole tonsil and lateral wall medially, with swelling behind the angle of the jaw.
w: Wrong - an intratonsillar abscess swells the tonsil itself, without the supratonsillar palatal bulge.
Wrong - retropharyngeal pus bulges the posterior pharyngeal wall, typically in a young child.
Wrong - parapharyngeal pus displaces the whole tonsil medially and causes swelling behind the angle of the mandible.
Wrong - submandibular (Ludwig's) infection raises the floor of mouth and tongue with a brawny neck swelling.
Correct - quinsy pus lies in the peritonsillar space, outside the capsule and inside the superior constrictor.

mcq.stem:
A 35-year-old woman with a right peritonsillar abscess is in the ENT procedure room. Topical and infiltrated local anaesthetic has been given and she is sitting upright.
Where should the incision for drainage be made?
o: Through the posterior pillar at the level of mid-tonsil
Low on the tonsil near its junction with the tongue base
Externally, through the skin behind the angle of the jaw
At the maximum bulge, above the upper pole of the tonsil
In the midline of the posterior pharyngeal wall
mcq.e: Drain at the **point of maximum bulge**, usually **above the upper pole**, where a horizontal line through the base of the uvula meets a vertical line along the anterior pillar. Keep the incision shallow (about 1 cm) and open the cavity bluntly, because the internal carotid artery lies about 2.5 cm posterolateral to the tonsil. Needle aspiration at the same point is diagnostic and often curative.
w: Wrong - the pus lies above and in front of the tonsil; the posterior pillar route misses it and heads towards the great vessels.
Wrong - quinsy collects at the upper pole, so a low incision misses the pus.
Wrong - external drainage is for parapharyngeal abscess, not quinsy.
Correct - incise at the maximum bulge above the upper pole, shallow and blunt.
Wrong - the posterior pharyngeal wall is the site for retropharyngeal collections, not peritonsillar ones.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old man has a 4-day history of left-sided throat pain following a bout of tonsillitis. Examination shows a bulging left soft palate with the uvula displaced to the right, and he can open his mouth only one fingerbreadth.
Spasm of which muscle chiefly causes his restricted mouth opening?
o: Medial pterygoid
Lateral pterygoid
Masseter
Temporalis
Superior constrictor
mcq.e: Trismus in quinsy comes from inflammation spreading through the superior constrictor to the **medial pterygoid**, which lies just lateral to it and is a jaw elevator; its spasm stops the mouth opening. Marked or worsening trismus suggests lateral spread and is a red flag for parapharyngeal extension. The lateral pterygoid opens the jaw, so its spasm would not lock it shut.
w: Correct - the medial pterygoid lies lateral to the superior constrictor and closes the jaw when irritated.
Wrong - the lateral pterygoid opens and protrudes the mandible and lies higher in the infratemporal fossa.
Wrong - the masseter lies superficially on the ramus; it is involved in dental or masseteric space infection.
Wrong - the temporalis lies far from the pharynx.
Wrong - the superior constrictor forms the lateral wall of the abscess but does not move the jaw.

mcq.stem:
A 22-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with 3 days of severe right-sided sore throat and odynophagia. There is diffuse redness and swelling of the right soft palate without a localised bulge, the uvula is midline and there is no trismus. Needle aspiration at the upper pole yields no pus.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Incision at the upper pole until pus is found
Immediate hot tonsillectomy under general anaesthetic
IV co-amoxiclav and fluids, then reassess in 24-48 h
External drainage through a transcervical incision
Discharge on oral penicillin with no follow-up
mcq.e: Diffuse palatal swelling without a pointing bulge, trismus or pus on aspiration is **peritonsillitis (peritonsillar cellulitis)**, the stage before an abscess forms. Treat with **IV antibiotics, fluids and analgesia** (a steroid may help) and reassess; if she has not improved in 24-48 hours, re-aspirate or request a **CECT neck** to look for a collection. Blind deep incision risks the great vessels.
w: Wrong - cutting blindly when there is no collection risks bleeding and does not treat cellulitis.
Wrong - hot tonsillectomy is an option for selected confirmed quinsy, not for cellulitis that may settle.
Correct - peritonsillitis is treated medically, with reassessment for abscess formation.
Wrong - transcervical drainage is for parapharyngeal abscess.
Wrong - severe unilateral peritonsillar infection needs review because it can progress to an abscess.

mcq.stem:
A 40-year-old man with no drug allergies has had 15 ml of foul-smelling pus drained from a left peritonsillar collection. He is dehydrated and cannot swallow tablets. Gram stain shows Gram-positive cocci and numerous Gram-negative anaerobic bacilli.
Which antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?
o: IV benzylpenicillin 1.2 g 6-hourly alone
IV co-amoxiclav 1.2 g every 8 hours
IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg once daily
Oral azithromycin 500 mg daily for 3 days
Oral metronidazole 400 mg 8-hourly
mcq.e: Quinsy pus contains **mixed aerobic (S. pyogenes, S. aureus) and anaerobic (Bacteroides, Fusobacterium)** flora, often with β-lactamase producers. **IV co-amoxiclav 1.2 g TDS** covers all of these, and the IV route suits a patient who cannot swallow; penicillin plus metronidazole (or clindamycin if allergic) is an alternative. Add IV fluids, analgesia and often a steroid, and switch to oral once he is swallowing.
w: Wrong - penicillin alone misses β-lactamase-producing staphylococci and some anaerobes.
Correct - co-amoxiclav covers streptococci, staphylococci and anaerobes, given IV.
Wrong - gentamicin has no anaerobic activity and poor streptococcal cover.
Wrong - oral therapy is impractical when he cannot swallow, and 3 days is too short for a deep abscess.
Wrong - metronidazole covers only anaerobes, missing the streptococci and staphylococci.

mcq.stem:
A 33-year-old man had a right quinsy treated by needle aspiration 3 days ago but is getting worse. He now has a temperature of 39 °C, a tender swelling behind the right angle of the mandible and painful neck stiffness, and the whole right tonsil and lateral pharyngeal wall are pushed towards the midline.
What is the most appropriate next investigation?
o: Repeat aspiration at the upper pole
Lateral soft-tissue neck radiograph
Orthopantomogram for a dental source
Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck
Bedside ultrasound of the neck
mcq.e: Medial displacement of the **whole tonsil and lateral pharyngeal wall**, swelling behind the angle of the jaw, torticollis and worsening sepsis after quinsy mean spread to the **parapharyngeal space**. **CECT neck** defines the collection, its relation to the carotid sheath and any extension to the retropharyngeal space or mediastinum, and guides **external (transcervical) drainage**. Other quinsy complications include laryngeal oedema, jugular vein thrombophlebitis and carotid haemorrhage.
w: Wrong - the pus is now lateral to the constrictor; another intraoral aspiration will not reach it safely.
Wrong - a lateral neck film assesses prevertebral (retropharyngeal) widening, not the lateral parapharyngeal space.
Wrong - a dental source is possible, but the urgent question is the extent of the deep neck collection.
Correct - CECT maps the parapharyngeal collection and its relation to the great vessels before drainage.
Wrong - ultrasound cannot reliably show the deep parapharyngeal space or mediastinal spread.

mcq.stem:
A 42-year-old man presents to the ED with 5 days of fever, odynophagia and neck pain that began after an infected, painful lower third molar. He has trismus and holds his neck stiffly. There is a tender, firm swelling behind the angle of the left mandible. Intraorally the left tonsil and lateral pharyngeal wall are displaced medially, but the tonsil itself is not inflamed and the uvula is central.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Left parapharyngeal space abscess
Left peritonsillar abscess (quinsy)
Acute retropharyngeal abscess
Ludwig's angina of the floor of mouth
Infected deep-lobe parotid tumour
mcq.e: Medial displacement of the tonsil and lateral pharyngeal wall with a normal-looking tonsil, plus swelling behind the angle of the jaw, places the pus lateral to the superior constrictor in the **parapharyngeal space**; teeth are a classic source (slide p36). In quinsy the tonsil itself is angry, the bulge is above the upper pole and the uvula is pushed to the opposite side. Trismus occurs in both (medial pterygoid irritation), so it does not discriminate.
w: Correct - medially pushed but normal-looking tonsil, swelling behind the jaw angle, trismus and a dental source = parapharyngeal abscess.
Wrong - quinsy gives an inflamed tonsil, bulging soft palate above the upper pole and a uvula deviated to the opposite side.
Wrong - retropharyngeal abscess bulges the POSTERIOR pharyngeal wall and is mainly a disease of young children.
Wrong - Ludwig's angina is bilateral submandibular/sublingual cellulitis with a raised, woody floor of mouth and tongue.
Wrong - a deep-lobe parotid tumour pushes the tonsil medially too but grows slowly and painlessly, without fever.

mcq.stem:
A 38-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes is admitted with a right deep neck abscess after tonsillitis. On day 2 his voice becomes hoarse and breathy, his tongue deviates to the right on protrusion, he cannot shrug his right shoulder, and he has right ptosis with a small right pupil.
Which compartment does the collection involve?
o: Prestyloid parapharyngeal compartment
Poststyloid parapharyngeal compartment
Retropharyngeal space in front of the alar fascia
Peritonsillar space lateral to the tonsil capsule
Danger space between alar and prevertebral fascia
mcq.e: The **poststyloid** compartment contains the carotid artery, internal jugular vein, **CN IX-XII** and the cervical **sympathetic chain** (slide p35). Vagal palsy (hoarseness), hypoglossal palsy (tongue deviates TOWARDS the lesion), accessory palsy (weak shrug) and Horner syndrome together localise there. The prestyloid compartment holds fat, the deep lobe of parotid, the maxillary artery and V3 branches, so it gives trismus and a medial tonsil bulge, not lower cranial nerve palsies.
w: Wrong - the prestyloid compartment contains fat, deep parotid, maxillary artery and V3 branches; no CN IX-XII or sympathetic chain.
Correct - CN X, XI and XII palsies plus Horner syndrome localise to the poststyloid compartment (carotid sheath contents and sympathetic chain).
Wrong - a retropharyngeal collection bulges the posterior pharyngeal wall and does not cause this cluster of cranial nerve palsies.
Wrong - quinsy lies between the tonsil capsule and superior constrictor, medial to the nerves; it gives trismus and uvular deviation.
Wrong - danger-space infection spreads down to the mediastinum; it does not selectively involve CN IX-XII and the sympathetic chain.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old woman with a right parapharyngeal abscess has had 48 hours of IV co-amoxiclav without improvement. She remains febrile with trismus and a tender swelling behind the angle of the jaw. CECT neck shows a 4 cm rim-enhancing collection in the poststyloid compartment, abutting the carotid sheath.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Needle aspiration through the anterior pillar under local anaesthesia
Transoral incision over the medial bulge of the lateral pharyngeal wall
Transcervical drainage through an external neck incision
Continue the same IV antibiotics for seven more days, then re-image
Incision at the point of maximum bulge above the upper tonsillar pole
mcq.e: A large abscess that fails 48 hours of IV antibiotics needs drainage, and for a **poststyloid** collection next to the carotid sheath the standard is an **external transcervical approach**, which gives control of the great vessels (slide p37). The transoral route is kept for small, accessible prestyloid collections well away from the carotid and jugular. Aspirating or incising above the tonsil treats quinsy, not a deep parapharyngeal collection.
w: Wrong - anterior pillar aspiration reaches the peritonsillar space; it cannot safely drain a poststyloid collection.
Wrong - transoral incision is only for small, accessible collections away from the great vessels; here it risks carotid injury.
Correct - an external transcervical incision drains large or poststyloid abscesses while protecting the carotid and internal jugular vein.
Wrong - a 4 cm abscess failing 48 h of IV antibiotics needs drainage; prolonging the same regimen risks spread and vessel erosion.
Wrong - incision at the point of maximum bulge above the upper pole is the quinsy technique, not for a parapharyngeal abscess.

mcq.stem:
A 24-year-old man is on the ward with a left parapharyngeal abscess. On day 3 he develops spiking fevers with rigors, a tender cord-like swelling along the anterior border of the left sternocleidomastoid, and pleuritic chest pain. Chest X-ray shows multiple small peripheral cavitating nodules.
Which complication is most likely?
o: Erosion of the internal carotid artery with sentinel bleeding
Spread of infection to the mediastinum along the carotid sheath
Acute laryngeal oedema with upper airway obstruction
Septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein
Extension into the retropharyngeal and danger spaces
mcq.e: Septic **thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein** throwing **septic emboli** to the lungs (Lemierre syndrome, classically Fusobacterium necrophorum) explains rigors, a tender cord along the sternocleidomastoid and cavitating lung nodules (slide p37: thrombophlebitis of jugular vein with septicaemia). Treat with prolonged IV antibiotics covering anaerobes and drain any collection. Carotid erosion presents with herald bleeds from the mouth or ear; mediastinitis with retrosternal pain and a widened mediastinum.
w: Wrong - carotid erosion presents with small herald bleeds from mouth or ear before torrential haemorrhage, not lung nodules.
Wrong - mediastinitis gives retrosternal pain, dyspnoea and a widened mediastinum rather than a tender cord and peripheral emboli.
Wrong - laryngeal oedema causes stridor and voice change; it does not explain rigors, a venous cord or cavitating nodules.
Correct - IJV septic thrombophlebitis (Lemierre) gives rigors, a tender cord along the SCM and septic pulmonary emboli.
Wrong - retropharyngeal or danger-space spread would bulge the posterior pharyngeal wall and track to the mediastinum.

mcq.stem:
A 2-year-old boy is referred from a Klinik Kesihatan after a week of URTI. He has fever, drools, refuses feeds, holds his neck extended and has a croupy cough with mild inspiratory stridor. Gentle examination shows a soft bulge of the posterior pharyngeal wall lying to the right of the midline.
Which anatomical feature best explains both his age group and the one-sided bulge?
o: A space running from the skull base to the diaphragm in front of the spine
The styloid process dividing the lateral space into two compartments
The superior constrictor separating the tonsil bed from the lateral space
Prevertebral fascia attached laterally to the cervical transverse processes
Paired nodes that regress by about age 4, either side of a midline raphe
mcq.e: Acute retropharyngeal abscess is suppuration of the **retropharyngeal (Rouvière) nodes**, which atrophy by about 3-5 years, so it is a disease of young children (slide p38). A midline fibrous raphe divides the space, so the abscess bulges to ONE side; a central bulge in an adult suggests a chronic TB (prevertebral) collection. Note: slide p38 gives the posterior boundary as prevertebral fascia; correct is the **alar fascia** - the danger space lies between alar and prevertebral fascia and leads to the mediastinum.
w: Wrong - this describes the danger space, which explains spread to the mediastinum, not the age group or lateral bulge.
Wrong - the styloid divides the parapharyngeal space into pre- and poststyloid compartments; irrelevant to a posterior wall bulge.
Wrong - the superior constrictor forms the lateral wall of the peritonsillar space, relevant to quinsy rather than this child.
Wrong - lateral attachment of the prevertebral fascia defines a central prevertebral (adult TB) abscess, not a one-sided bulge.
Correct - Rouvière nodes regress in early childhood and lie either side of the median raphe, hence young children and a lateral bulge.

mcq.stem:
An 18-month-old girl has 3 days of fever, drooling, neck stiffness and noisy breathing after a cold. She sits comfortably on her mother's lap with SpO2 97% on air. A lateral soft-tissue neck X-ray is taken with the neck extended during inspiration.
Which finding would best support the most likely diagnosis?
o: Prevertebral soft tissue at C2 thicker than 7 mm
Swollen, rounded epiglottis giving a 'thumb sign'
Ballooned hypopharynx with subglottic narrowing
Round radio-opaque disc at the cricopharyngeus
Large adenoid pad narrowing the nasopharynx
mcq.e: In children the prevertebral soft tissue at C2 should be less than about **7 mm** (roughly 14 mm at C6); widening, sometimes with a gas-fluid level or loss of lordosis, suggests a **retropharyngeal abscess**. The film must be taken in extension on inspiration, because flexion or expiration falsely widens the shadow. CECT neck then distinguishes abscess from cellulitis and shows the extent (slide p39).
w: Correct - widened prevertebral soft tissue on a properly taken lateral film supports a retropharyngeal collection.
Wrong - the thumb sign is acute epiglottitis: toxic, sitting forward, rapidly progressive, usually without neck stiffness.
Wrong - subglottic narrowing with hypopharyngeal ballooning suggests croup, which gives barking cough without drooling or neck stiffness.
Wrong - a radio-opaque disc at cricopharyngeus is an ingested coin; there would be a history of sudden onset, not fever after a cold.
Wrong - adenoid hypertrophy causes chronic mouth breathing and snoring, not acute fever, drooling and neck stiffness.

mcq.stem:
A 3-year-old boy with fever, drooling and stridor has a CECT neck showing a 3 cm rim-enhancing collection in the retropharyngeal space to one side of the midline, with no mediastinal extension. He is tiring but maintains SpO2 94% on oxygen.
What is the most appropriate definitive management?
o: IV antibiotics alone with close ward observation for 72 hours
Secure the airway, then intraoral drainage with the head down
External drainage through an incision behind the sternomastoid
Needle aspiration through the anterior pillar under local anaesthetic
Antituberculous therapy and an MRI scan of the cervical spine
mcq.e: A large acute retropharyngeal abscess with airway compromise needs drainage: **secure the airway first** (intubation by an experienced anaesthetist, tracheostomy if that fails), then incise the bulge **intraorally** with the child **head-down (Rose's position)** so pus does not spill into the larynx (slides p39-40). Antibiotics alone are reserved for small collections or cellulitis in a stable child. External drainage behind the sternomastoid is the route for chronic TB abscesses.
w: Wrong - antibiotics alone suit small collections or cellulitis; a 3 cm abscess in a tiring child with stridor needs drainage.
Correct - airway first, then intraoral incision in the head-down position to prevent aspiration of pus.
Wrong - the external route behind the sternomastoid is for chronic (TB) retropharyngeal abscess, to avoid a chronic sinus.
Wrong - anterior pillar aspiration drains a peritonsillar abscess and cannot reach the retropharyngeal space.
Wrong - antituberculous therapy is for the chronic adult type with cervical spine caries, not acute nodal suppuration in a child.

mcq.stem:
A 34-year-old man presents to ENT clinic with 3 months of throat discomfort, mild dysphagia, neck stiffness, night sweats and 6 kg weight loss. The posterior pharyngeal wall shows a smooth, fluctuant swelling in the midline. There is tenderness over the lower cervical spine, and X-ray shows narrowing of the C4-C5 disc space with vertebral erosion.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Intraoral incision over the bulge followed by oral co-amoxiclav
Transoral drainage in the head-down position with IV ceftriaxone
Antituberculous therapy with drainage via an external neck incision
Repeated transoral needle aspiration with a soft cervical collar
Urgent tracheostomy followed by palliative neck radiotherapy
mcq.e: A slow, **central** prevertebral collection in an adult with vertebral erosion is a **chronic retropharyngeal (cold) abscess** from cervical spine TB (Pott's disease) or caseous nodes (slide p39). Give antituberculous therapy and, when drainage is needed, use an **external approach behind the sternocleidomastoid** - an intraoral incision risks a persistent pharyngeal sinus and secondary infection. Spinal review is needed for stability. Note: slide p39 says only 'incision and drainage'; for the chronic type this should be external, not transoral.
w: Wrong - intraoral incision of a TB cold abscess leaves a chronic pharyngeal sinus, and co-amoxiclav does not treat tuberculosis.
Wrong - transoral head-down drainage is the technique for acute pyogenic abscess in children, not adult spinal TB.
Correct - treat the TB with antituberculous therapy and drain externally behind the sternocleidomastoid to avoid a sinus.
Wrong - repeated transoral aspiration risks a chronic sinus and leaves the spinal tuberculosis untreated.
Wrong - his airway is not compromised and this is infection, not malignancy; tracheostomy and radiotherapy are inappropriate.

mcq.stem:
A 61-year-old man, a heavy smoker and drinker, attends ENT clinic with 2 months of right otalgia, mild odynophagia and a muffled voice. Otoscopy is normal. There is a hard, painless 3 cm right upper neck node. Bimanual palpation reveals an indurated mass at the right tongue base, and flexible laryngoscopy shows an ulcerated exophytic growth there.
Which investigation establishes the diagnosis?
o: Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the neck and thorax
Open excision biopsy of the right neck node
PET-CT scan to look for distant metastases
Biopsy of the tongue-base lesion for histology
MRI of the oropharynx and the skull base
mcq.e: The diagnosis is **histological** - biopsy the primary (at endoscopy or EUA) for HPE (slide p47); CT, MRI and PET-CT stage the disease but do not prove it. Otalgia with a normal ear in a smoker is referred pain via **CN IX** from the tongue base or tonsil until proven otherwise. Open biopsy of a neck node before the primary is found is a classic trap: it seeds the neck and compromises later neck dissection; FNAC or core biopsy is used for the node instead.
w: Wrong - CT stages local extent, nodes and chest disease but cannot give a tissue diagnosis.
Wrong - open node biopsy risks tumour seeding and spoils the later neck dissection; sample the primary (and FNAC the node).
Wrong - PET-CT detects metastases and occult primaries; it does not establish histology.
Correct - biopsy of the visible primary for histopathology confirms squamous cell carcinoma.
Wrong - MRI defines soft-tissue extent for staging and planning but is not diagnostic.

mcq.stem:
A 44-year-old non-smoking accountant notices a painless, soft, cystic lump in the left upper neck. Examination shows a small, firm left tonsil with no ulceration. Tonsil biopsy shows squamous cell carcinoma that stains strongly for p16.
Compared with tobacco-related oropharyngeal carcinoma, which statement about this tumour is correct?
o: It is mainly driven by low-risk HPV types 6 and 11
It typically affects elderly heavy smokers and drinkers
It only rarely spreads to the cervical lymph nodes
It is staged with the same AJCC 8th edition TNM tables
It responds better to treatment, with better survival
mcq.e: p16-positive oropharyngeal SCC is driven by **high-risk HPV-16**, affects younger non-smokers, often presents with a **cystic neck node** from a small primary, and has much **better survival** after (chemo)radiotherapy or TORS; AJCC 8th edition stages it separately from p16-negative disease. HPV 6 and 11 are low-risk types causing benign papillomas (slide p43). A cystic lateral neck mass in an adult over 40 is HPV-related SCC until proven otherwise, not a branchial cyst.
w: Wrong - HPV 6 and 11 cause benign papillomas; HPV-related SCC is driven mainly by high-risk HPV-16.
Wrong - that is the profile of tobacco/alcohol-related disease; HPV-positive patients are younger and often non-smokers.
Wrong - early cystic nodal metastasis from a small primary is typical of HPV-positive tumours.
Wrong - AJCC 8th edition has separate, more favourable staging for p16-positive oropharyngeal cancer.
Correct - HPV-positive tumours are more radio- and chemosensitive and carry a much better prognosis.

mcq.stem:
A 56-year-old woman is referred from a Klinik Kesihatan with 6 weeks of a 'lump in the throat'. She has no fever or sore throat but reports night sweats. The left tonsil is markedly larger than the right, firm and smooth, without exudate or ulceration. There is a 2 cm rubbery left level II node.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Tonsillectomy as an excision biopsy for histology
Penicillin V for 10 days and review in clinic
Incision and drainage of the left tonsil under LA
Reassurance with a routine review in three months
Throat swab culture and a Monospot blood test
mcq.e: Unilateral tonsillar enlargement in an adult, especially with night sweats or a node, is **malignancy (lymphoma or SCC) until proven otherwise**; suspicion of malignancy is an absolute indication for tonsillectomy (slide p28), and lymphoma is one of the histological types (slide p45). The specimen goes fresh for histology and flow cytometry. Antibiotic trials or watchful waiting only delay the diagnosis; incision and drainage is for quinsy, which is acutely painful and febrile.
w: Correct - excision tonsillectomy gives the whole specimen for histology, essential to diagnose lymphoma or carcinoma.
Wrong - she has no infective features; an antibiotic trial delays diagnosis of a probable malignancy.
Wrong - there is no abscess; I&D is for quinsy, which presents with acute pain, fever and trismus.
Wrong - an asymmetric firm tonsil with night sweats and a node must not be watched.
Wrong - swab and Monospot investigate infective sore throat in younger patients, not an afebrile asymmetric tonsil.

mcq.stem:
A 26-year-old woman attends ENT clinic with intermittent blood-stained saliva and mild dysphagia. There is a soft, bluish, compressible lesion on the right lateral pharyngeal wall extending onto the tonsil, which has enlarged over the past year.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Punch biopsy in clinic to confirm the histology
Sclerotherapy or laser coagulation of the lesion
Observation, as such lesions involute in adulthood
Incision and drainage of the swelling under LA
Wide excision with postoperative radiotherapy
mcq.e: A soft, bluish, compressible lesion is a **haemangioma** (capillary or cavernous). Treat when it enlarges, bleeds or causes dysphagia, using **sclerotherapy, cryotherapy or laser coagulation** (slide p43). Avoid clinic biopsy or incision - it can bleed torrentially. Involution is a feature of infantile haemangiomas, not enlarging adult lesions. Note: slides p42-43 say 'laryngeal wall/arch'; correct is posterior and lateral **pharyngeal** wall.
w: Wrong - biopsy of a vascular lesion risks severe haemorrhage; the clinical picture (plus imaging if needed) suffices.
Correct - an enlarging, bleeding haemangioma is treated with sclerotherapy, cryotherapy or laser coagulation.
Wrong - spontaneous involution is typical of infantile haemangiomas; this adult lesion is growing and bleeding.
Wrong - this is not a collection; incising a haemangioma causes brisk bleeding.
Wrong - it is benign; wide excision with radiotherapy is cancer treatment and is unnecessary.

mcq.stem:
A 63-year-old man who smokes has biopsy-proven p16-negative squamous cell carcinoma of the left tonsil. Examination under anaesthesia and MRI show a 3.5 cm primary extending onto the lingual surface of the epiglottis, with no invasion of the larynx, extrinsic tongue muscles, medial pterygoid, hard palate or mandible.
What is the T stage?
o: T1
T2
T3
T4a
T4b
mcq.e: For p16-negative oropharyngeal SCC: **T1 ≤ 2 cm, T2 > 2-4 cm, T3 > 4 cm or extension to the lingual surface of the epiglottis**, T4a invades the larynx, extrinsic tongue muscles, medial pterygoid, hard palate or mandible, and T4b the lateral pterygoid, pterygoid plates, skull base or encases the carotid. Size alone (3.5 cm) would make it T2, but spread onto the lingual epiglottis upstages it to T3. p16-positive tumours use separate AJCC 8th edition tables.
w: Wrong - T1 is 2 cm or less in greatest dimension.
Wrong - 3.5 cm alone would be T2, but extension onto the lingual surface of the epiglottis upstages it.
Correct - extension to the lingual surface of the epiglottis makes it T3 regardless of size.
Wrong - T4a requires invasion of larynx, extrinsic tongue muscles, medial pterygoid, hard palate or mandible.
Wrong - T4b requires lateral pterygoid, pterygoid plates, lateral nasopharynx, skull base or carotid encasement.

mcq.stem:
A 48-year-old woman notices a painless swelling of the palate that has grown slowly over 2 years. There is a firm, smooth, 2 cm submucosal mass at the junction of the left hard and soft palate, with intact mucosa and no neck nodes. Biopsy shows a mixed epithelial and myxoid stromal tumour.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Incision and drainage through the overlying mucosa
Enucleation of the mass through a mucosal incision
Radiotherapy alone, to avoid a palatal defect
Wide local excision with a cuff of normal tissue
Observation, as it has no malignant potential
mcq.e: This is a **pleomorphic adenoma of the minor palatal salivary glands** (slide p44). It has an incomplete capsule with finger-like projections, so enucleation leaves tumour behind and it recurs; the treatment is **complete wide excision** with a margin (often including periosteum). It is potentially malignant (carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma), so observation is wrong, and it is not managed with primary radiotherapy.
w: Wrong - it is a solid tumour, not a cyst or abscess; incision achieves nothing and seeds tumour.
Wrong - pseudopod extensions through the incomplete capsule make enucleation prone to recurrence.
Wrong - pleomorphic adenoma is treated surgically; radiotherapy is not primary treatment for this benign tumour.
Correct - wide local excision with a margin of normal tissue prevents recurrence of a palatal pleomorphic adenoma.
Wrong - pleomorphic adenoma can undergo malignant change, so it should be excised.

mcq.stem:
A 56-year-old woman is seen at a Klinik Kesihatan because her husband complains of her loud snoring. She feels refreshed during the day and he has never noticed pauses in her breathing. She takes amlodipine for hypertension. BMI is 32 kg/m² and neck circumference is 43 cm.
What is her STOP-BANG score and the most appropriate action?
o: Score 2; low risk, so give weight-loss advice only
Score 3; low risk, so repeat the questionnaire yearly
Score 5; high risk, so start CPAP without a sleep study
Score 6; high risk, so refer directly for tonsillectomy
Score 4; intermediate risk, so refer for a sleep study
mcq.e: S1 (loud snoring) + T0 + O0 + P1 (treated hypertension) + B0 (BMI not > 35) + A1 (> 50) + N1 (> 40 cm) + G0 = **4**. STOP-BANG 0-2 is low, 3-4 intermediate and 5-8 high risk; a score of **≥ 3** warrants objective sleep testing. Note: slide p56 writes 'STOP-BANG > 3'; the standard cut-off is ≥ 3. STOP-BANG screens - it never replaces a sleep study before CPAP or surgery.
w: Wrong - this misses the age and neck points; the score is 4.
Wrong - the score is 4, and a score of 3 is already intermediate risk needing referral, not low risk.
Wrong - BMI 32 does not score (cut-off > 35) and she is female; even high scores need a diagnostic study before CPAP.
Wrong - the score is 4, and there is no tonsillar hypertrophy; surgery is never planned from a questionnaire.
Correct - snoring, pressure, age > 50 and neck > 40 cm give 4 (intermediate risk), so refer for a diagnostic sleep study.

mcq.stem:
A 48-year-old taxi driver is referred because his wife has witnessed long pauses in his breathing. He nearly fell asleep at a traffic light last week. Epworth Sleepiness Scale is 16, BMI 38 kg/m² and neck circumference 45 cm. Overnight pulse oximetry alone (one channel) at the district hospital was reported as normal.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Attended level 1 polysomnography in a sleep laboratory
Reassure him that overnight oximetry has excluded OSA
Repeat the Epworth Sleepiness Scale in three months
Drug-induced sleep endoscopy to grade the obstruction
Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty with a tonsillectomy
mcq.e: Single- or dual-channel oximetry is a **level 4** study - screening only, it cannot exclude OSA (slide p57). With a high pre-test probability (witnessed apnoeas, ESS 16 > 10, BMI 38), a negative, inconclusive or inadequate limited study must be followed by full **polysomnography**; only levels 1-3 can diagnose. He must be advised not to drive while sleepy until treated. DISE and surgery come only after OSA is confirmed and CPAP has been considered.
w: Correct - a negative level 4 study with high clinical suspicion must be followed by full polysomnography.
Wrong - level 4 oximetry is a screening tool and cannot exclude OSA in a high-probability patient.
Wrong - ESS only measures sleepiness; repeating it delays diagnosis in a sleepy professional driver.
Wrong - DISE localises collapse before surgery; it is not used to diagnose OSA.
Wrong - surgery is not planned before OSA is confirmed and CPAP, the first-line treatment, is considered.

mcq.stem:
A 45-year-old man undergoes polysomnography as part of a research screening programme. He has no complaints of snoring or daytime sleepiness (ESS 4) and no hypertension, diabetes or cardiac disease. His apnoea-hypopnoea index is 22 events/hour, mostly obstructive.
What is the correct interpretation?
o: Not OSA, because he has no symptoms or comorbidity
Moderate OSA, diagnosed even without any symptoms
Mild OSA, but only if symptoms develop in future
Severe OSA, as the index is above 20 events/hour
Primary snoring with no apnoea-related disease
mcq.e: Adult OSA is diagnosed with **AHI ≥ 5 plus** typical symptoms or associated disease, or **AHI ≥ 15 regardless of symptoms** (slide p58). Severity: mild 5 to < 15, moderate 15-30, severe > 30 events/hour, so 22 is moderate. ESS measures subjective sleepiness, not airway collapse, so a low ESS does not exclude OSA.
w: Wrong - symptoms are only needed when AHI is 5-14; an AHI of 15 or more is diagnostic on its own.
Correct - AHI 15-30 is moderate OSA, and AHI ≥ 15 is diagnostic even without symptoms.
Wrong - 22 is above the mild range (5 to < 15) and the diagnosis does not wait for symptoms.
Wrong - severe OSA is AHI > 30 events/hour.
Wrong - primary snoring has no significant apnoeas or desaturation; his AHI is 22.

mcq.stem:
A 40-year-old woman with BMI 46 kg/m² presents with hypersomnolence, morning headaches and ankle swelling. Spirometry, chest X-ray and thyroid function are normal. An awake arterial blood gas on room air shows pH 7.37, PaCO2 56 mmHg, PaO2 62 mmHg and a raised bicarbonate.
Which diagnosis best explains the daytime blood gas?
o: Obstructive sleep apnoea alone
Central sleep apnoea from opioids
Obesity hypoventilation syndrome
Primary snoring with nasal blockage
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
mcq.e: **Obesity hypoventilation syndrome** = BMI ≥ 30 + awake daytime **PaCO2 > 45 mmHg** with other causes of hypoventilation excluded (normal spirometry, chest X-ray and thyroid) (slide p60). Most OHS patients also have OSA, but OSA alone does not cause daytime hypercapnia; the raised bicarbonate shows chronic CO2 retention and ankle oedema hints at cor pulmonale. These patients often need BiPAP rather than CPAP.
w: Wrong - OSA causes nocturnal desaturation, but daytime PaCO2 stays normal unless OHS coexists.
Wrong - there is no opioid use, and central apnoea does not explain obesity-related daytime hypercapnia.
Correct - BMI ≥ 30 with awake PaCO2 > 45 mmHg and other causes excluded defines OHS.
Wrong - primary snoring causes no apnoeas, desaturation or blood gas abnormality.
Wrong - normal spirometry excludes COPD as the cause of hypercapnia.

mcq.stem:
A 69-year-old man with ischaemic heart failure (ejection fraction 25%) is referred for disturbed sleep. He is not obese and takes no opioids. Polysomnography shows repeated cycles of waxing and waning breathing with 20-second pauses, during which both airflow and chest and abdominal belt movements are absent.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Obstructive sleep apnoea
Obesity hypoventilation
Mixed sleep apnoea
Central sleep apnoea
Upper airway resistance syndrome
mcq.e: In **central apnoea** the airway is open but the brainstem stops driving the respiratory muscles, so airflow AND respiratory effort are both absent (slide p52); in heart failure this takes the crescendo-decrescendo **Cheyne-Stokes** pattern (slide p60). In obstructive apnoea effort continues, often with paradoxical chest-abdominal movement, against a closed airway. Mixed apnoea starts central and ends with obstructed efforts.
w: Wrong - in obstructive apnoea chest and abdominal effort continue while airflow stops.
Wrong - he is not obese, and OHS is defined by awake daytime hypercapnia, not this PSG pattern.
Wrong - mixed apnoea begins without effort but ends with obstructed breathing efforts.
Correct - absent airflow AND absent effort in a waxing-waning pattern with heart failure = central (Cheyne-Stokes) apnoea.
Wrong - upper airway resistance causes effort-related arousals with increasing effort, not absent effort.

mcq.stem:
A 45-year-old woman is referred with loud snoring, daytime fatigue and 8 kg weight gain over a year. She also reports cold intolerance, constipation and a hoarse voice. Examination shows dry skin, an enlarged tongue, a puffy face and slow-relaxing ankle reflexes. BMI is 31 kg/m².
Alongside a sleep study, which blood test is most important to request?
o: Glycated haemoglobin
Morning serum cortisol
Serum IGF-1 level
Serum ferritin level
TSH and free T4
mcq.e: Weight gain, cold intolerance, hoarseness, macroglossia and slow-relaxing reflexes point to **hypothyroidism**, an endocrine cause of OSA (slide p52) through macroglossia, mucopolysaccharide deposition in the pharynx and reduced ventilatory drive. Treating it with thyroxine can improve or resolve the OSA. IGF-1 screens for acromegaly, which also causes macroglossia and OSA, but she has hypothyroid rather than acromegalic features.
w: Wrong - diabetes screening is reasonable in obesity but does not explain her hypothyroid features.
Wrong - cortisol tests for Cushing's syndrome; she has no striae, proximal myopathy or plethora.
Wrong - IGF-1 tests for acromegaly, which also gives macroglossia, but she lacks coarse features or enlarging hands.
Wrong - ferritin looks for iron deficiency in restless legs; it does not explain this picture.
Correct - hypothyroidism is a treatable cause of OSA; TSH and free T4 confirm it.

mcq.stem:
A 52-year-old man with loud snoring completes the Epworth Sleepiness Scale at ENT clinic. His scores are: sitting and reading 2, watching TV 3, sitting inactive in a public place 2, car passenger for an hour 3, lying down in the afternoon 3, sitting and talking 0, sitting quietly after lunch 2, in a car stopped in traffic 1.
What is the correct interpretation?
o: 16; excessive sleepiness, so arrange a sleep study
16; this confirms moderate OSA, so start CPAP
14; borderline sleepiness, so repeat in 6 months
8; normal daytime sleepiness, so take no action
16; this indicates severe OSA, so refer for UPPP
mcq.e: ESS has 8 situations each scored 0-3 (total 0-24); his total is **16**, and **> 10 indicates excessive daytime sleepiness** (slide p56). ESS measures subjective sleepiness only - it is **not diagnostic** of OSA and does not grade severity, so the next step is objective sleep testing, not treatment. Severity comes from the AHI.
w: Correct - 16 is above 10 (excessive sleepiness), and objective sleep testing is needed to diagnose OSA.
Wrong - ESS is not diagnostic and cannot grade OSA; CPAP needs a confirmed diagnosis.
Wrong - the total is 16, not 14, and either score is above 10, not borderline.
Wrong - the total is 16; 8 would be within normal limits.
Wrong - ESS cannot grade severity, and surgery is never planned from a questionnaire.

mcq.stem:
A 38-year-old man with moderate OSA (AHI 24 events/hour) has stopped CPAP after 6 months despite mask refits and humidification. BMI is 27 kg/m². He has a modified Mallampati grade 3 and grade 2 tonsils, and wants surgery.
Which assessment most accurately identifies the level and pattern of airway collapse before surgery?
o: Awake nasendoscopy with Müller's manoeuvre
Drug-induced sleep endoscopy
Lateral cephalometric radiograph
Repeat attended polysomnography
Awake CT scan of the upper airway
mcq.e: **DISE** reproduces sleep-like muscle relaxation with propofol or midazolam, showing the site (palate, oropharynx, tongue base, epiglottis) and pattern of collapse (slide p59). The Malaysian CPG considers it more accurate than awake **FNMM** (Müller's manoeuvre), which is a fallback when DISE is not possible. Awake imaging misses dynamic collapse, and PSG quantifies severity but cannot localise the obstruction.
w: Wrong - awake FNMM is less accurate than DISE and is offered only when DISE cannot be performed.
Correct - DISE shows the site and degree of dynamic collapse under sedation and guides sleep surgery.
Wrong - cephalometry shows skeletal relationships but not dynamic soft-tissue collapse during sleep.
Wrong - PSG measures severity (AHI) but cannot localise the level of obstruction.
Wrong - an awake static scan misses the collapse that only happens with sleep-related muscle relaxation.

mcq.stem:
A 50-year-old lorry driver has polysomnography showing AHI 38 events/hour with nadir SpO2 78%. ESS is 15, BMI 33 kg/m², and he has hypertension. His tonsils are grade 1 and his nasal airway is clear.
What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
o: Mandibular advancement device fitted by a dentist
Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty under general anaesthesia
Nightly CPAP, with weight-loss and driving advice
Positional therapy with the tennis-ball technique
Tracheostomy to bypass the obstructed upper airway
mcq.e: AHI > 30 is **severe OSA**; **CPAP** is the gold-standard first-line treatment for moderate-severe disease, pneumatically splinting the whole pharynx, combined with weight loss, avoiding alcohol and sedatives, and advice not to drive while sleepy. Mandibular advancement suits mild-moderate or CPAP-intolerant OSA, UPPP succeeds poorly with small tonsils and obesity, and tracheostomy is the last resort (slide p61).
w: Wrong - a mandibular advancement device is for mild-moderate OSA or CPAP intolerance, not first-line in severe disease.
Wrong - UPPP has a low success rate in severe OSA with obesity and small tonsils, and is not first-line.
Correct - CPAP is first-line for severe OSA, with lifestyle measures and driving safety advice.
Wrong - positional therapy alone is for mild, supine-predominant OSA, not severe disease.
Wrong - tracheostomy is curative but reserved as the last resort when other treatments fail.

mcq.stem:
A 44-year-old man with severe OSA cannot use CPAP for more than an hour a night because of nasal blockage and mouth leak. Anterior rhinoscopy shows a septal deviation to the left and bilateral inferior turbinate hypertrophy. He is booked for septoplasty and inferior turbinate reduction.
What is the main expected benefit of this surgery?
o: Cure of the OSA, so that CPAP can be stopped
Normalisation of the AHI in most patients
No further need for a follow-up sleep study
Better CPAP tolerance at a lower pressure
Prevention of tongue-base collapse in REM sleep
mcq.e: Nasal surgery lowers nasal resistance (slide p63), which improves CPAP comfort and adherence and may lower the pressure needed, but it seldom cures OSA because collapse occurs at the palate and tongue base. He should continue CPAP and have treatment efficacy re-assessed. Expecting a normal AHI after septoplasty alone is the trap.
w: Wrong - nasal surgery rarely cures OSA; collapse is mainly retropalatal and retroglossal.
Wrong - the AHI usually changes little after isolated nasal surgery.
Wrong - he still has severe OSA and needs ongoing CPAP with review of its effectiveness.
Correct - reducing nasal resistance improves CPAP tolerance and may lower the pressure required.
Wrong - nasal surgery does not affect tongue-base collapse, which worsens in REM sleep.

mcq.stem:
A 5-year-old boy of normal weight has loud nightly snoring, witnessed pauses, restless sleep, bedwetting and poor concentration at school. He mouth-breathes, his tonsils are grade 4 and meet in the midline, and a lateral neck X-ray shows a large adenoid. Polysomnography shows an obstructive AHI of 12 events/hour.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Nightly CPAP through a nasal mask
Intranasal steroid alone for a year
Custom mandibular advancement device
Weight-reduction programme and review
Adenotonsillectomy
mcq.e: In children an obstructive **AHI > 1** is abnormal and AHI 12 is severe; with adenotonsillar hypertrophy, **adenotonsillectomy is first-line** (obstructive hypertrophy is an absolute indication, slide p28). Intranasal steroids are an option only for mild disease or as a bridge, and CPAP is for children unfit for or failing surgery. Severe paediatric OSA needs overnight post-operative monitoring because of respiratory complications.
w: Wrong - CPAP is for children unfit for surgery or with residual OSA after adenotonsillectomy.
Wrong - intranasal steroids help mild paediatric OSA only; AHI 12 with grade 4 tonsils needs surgery.
Wrong - oral appliances are not used in a growing 5-year-old with adenotonsillar obstruction.
Wrong - he is of normal weight; the cause is adenotonsillar hypertrophy.
Correct - adenotonsillectomy is first-line for paediatric OSA due to adenotonsillar hypertrophy.

mcq.stem:
A 41-year-old man is brought by his wife, who now sleeps in another room because of his snoring. Polysomnography shows AHI 11 events/hour with mainly supine events; ESS is 9. BMI is 25 kg/m². He has a retruded mandible, healthy teeth and small tonsils, and found CPAP intolerable after a 2-month trial.
What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Custom mandibular advancement device
Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty
Maxillomandibular advancement surgery
Tracheostomy
Referral for bariatric surgery
mcq.e: A **mandibular advancement appliance** holds the mandible and tongue forward, enlarging the retroglossal airway; it suits **mild-moderate OSA** or CPAP intolerance, especially with retrognathia and good teeth (slide p61). Positional therapy can be added for supine-predominant events. Maxillomandibular advancement is for severe OSA failing other options, bariatric surgery for obesity, and tracheostomy is the last resort. Treatment also relieves the bed partner ('spouse syndrome', slide p65).
w: Correct - mild OSA, CPAP intolerance, retrognathia and healthy teeth make a mandibular advancement device ideal.
Wrong - UPPP has limited success, especially with small tonsils and retroglossal (retrognathic) narrowing.
Wrong - maxillomandibular advancement is major skeletal surgery for severe OSA failing other treatments.
Wrong - tracheostomy is the last resort for severe, refractory OSA, not mild disease.
Wrong - his BMI is 25, so bariatric surgery has no role.
